text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday vetoed legislation that would have narrowed exemptions to the California Environmental Quality Act for advanced manufacturing facilities amid pushback from business and industry groups.

Senate Bill 954 from state Sen. Catherine Blakespear (D-Encinitas) would have rolled back parts of last year’s controversial overhaul of CEQA, which fast-tracked approvals for a broad array of housing and infrastructure projects in an effort to ease new construction in the state.

Critics said the overhaul opened up a path for advanced manufacturing facilities such as strip miners, chemical producers, battery recyclers and semiconductor plants to open in communities without any environmental review. Dozens of environmental groups including the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council and California Environmental Voters urged the governor to sign the legislation into law, arguing that it would have provided essential protections for communities that already experience the worst pollution from industrial facilities.

In his veto message, Newsom said last year’s CEQA reform was a “long overdue overhaul to get California building again.”

“While I appreciate the author’s stated intent to ensure these reforms do not result in unintended adverse impacts on the environment, this bill does not merely clarify or refine the existing exemption. It repeals the CEQA exemption for advanced manufacturing facilities,” the governor wrote. “Further, the bill’s numerous new siting, operational, and emissions requirements would make the narrower exemption impractical for many of the projects it was intended to support.”

In a statement, Blakespear said she was disappointed in the decision. While some of the new CEQA exemptions are important to stimulate construction, the recent near-miss chemical disaster in Garden Grove — which prompted thousands of evacuations in May — illustrates the danger that can come from siting advanced manufacturing facilities in communities, she said.

“We should not have to wait for another emergency before recognizing that sweeping — and rushed — exemptions from environmental review need reasonable guardrails,” Blakespear said. “Protecting communities and workers is not an impediment to economic growth; it is part of responsible growth. We need guardrails to these CEQA exemptions to safeguard Californians and ensure the environment isn’t damaged.”

Newsom’s veto came amid pushback from industry groups and prominent business organizations including the California Chamber of Commerce and the California Manufacturers & Technology Assn. The California Department of Finance also was opposed to the bill, which it described in an analysis as “inconsistent with Administration policy.”

Lance Hastings, chief executive of the California Manufacturers & Technology Assn., said in a statement Friday that the governor’s veto protects “the ability of manufacturers to innovate and create here in California.”

Manufacturing generates $382 billion a year for California and supports 1.24 million jobs, he said.

But opponents said Newsom’s decision ultimately will endanger communities and leave more people exposed to industrial hazards.

“Frontline communities across California continue to face consequences from polluting industries that have damaged our air and water for the sake of corporate profit,” said Asha Sharma, deputy director at the nonprofit Sierra Club California. “SB 954 was developed to ensure those same mistakes do not continue.”

Blakespear said she will continue working on the issue next year.

text:
Where The Two Powertrains Diverge

The technical reasons hybrids are winning the moment are worth spelling out, because they explain why the category has staying power beyond a single incentive cycle. Hybrid electric vehicles that never plug in hold the dominant share, recovering energy through regenerative braking and appealing to buyers who want fuel savings without changing how they refuel. That charging independence is the single most durable advantage.

Mild-hybrid systems are spreading fastest through the segments where full electrification struggles. A small electric motor delivers high-single-digit to low-double-digit fuel savings at a fraction of a full hybrid's cost, and mild hybrids are increasingly standard on pickups and larger vehicles where they preserve towing and payload. Silicon-carbide power electronics and improved battery management are raising hybrid efficiency further, narrowing the everyday gap with battery-electric operation.

The restraints on hybrids are real but slow-moving. Fleet-emission rules that reward zero-tailpipe operation can favor battery-electric and plug-in models, and falling battery prices may eventually narrow the hybrid cost advantage. For now, though, affordability, fuel efficiency, and model availability are carrying the segment, and the growth is expected to come from wider model coverage rather than any single subsidy.

title: EPA Guts Clean Air Rules, Enables AI Data Center Pollution - Earthjustice
description:

This loophole has helped to fuel the recent explosion of AI data centers and health- and climate-harming pollution.
AI data centers are trying to evade oversight by utility regulators by building their own private power plants.
This new guidance violates Clean Air Act requirements that enforceable offsetting reductions be secured before issuance of construction permits.
Instead, the EPA continues to abandon its mandate to protect our health, instead offering handouts to industrial polluters and AI data centers.
text:
The administration’s response to growing opposition to AI data centers has been to limit the public’s right to be heard, and to weaken environmental regulations. Last year, the administration vowed to repeal or weaken any regulations that hinder AI deployment and to promote the rapid buildout of data centers across the United States. The assault on the Clean Air Act on behalf of AI data centers escalated in recent months, including four actions that would severely undermine key pollution protections, exclude the public, and speed the construction of data centers and the power plants that supply their electricity.

Cutting out the public and bypassing the Clean Air Act

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) seeks to eliminate a longstanding requirement that the public be notified and have input on applications for air pollution permits for a variety of industrial facilities, including some new AI data centers and their power plants. This would mean residents might not even learn about air pollution at proposed new AI data centers before construction starts. This type of “minor source” permit applies to all kinds of facilities, from chemical plants to sterilizers to hazardous waste combustors. The pollution from these facilities is often not “minor,” as they may still emit up to 250 tons of dangerous pollutants per year.

Since these permits require less stringent review, companies powering AI data centers may seek to artificially divide large projects into smaller ones to qualify for a so-called “minor” permit that would minimize pollution reductions required under law. This loophole has helped to fuel the recent explosion of AI data centers and health- and climate-harming pollution. If finalized, the administration’s new rule will supercharge the existing loophole by keeping the public in the dark about plans for new industrial pollution in their backyard.

EPA’s longstanding requirement allowing public participation reflects the reality that public review improves permitting decisions by identifying underestimated emissions, inadequate pollution limits, insufficient air quality impacts analyses, and other errors before construction begins. EPA’s proposal would instead authorize state and local air agencies to issue preconstruction air pollution permits without any public notice or opportunity for comment. Environmental and public health groups filed extensive comments opposing EPA’s proposal.

Exempting plants from acid rain limits

In July, EPA released a memo that proposed to exempt generators that are not connected to the grid from acid rain requirements. AI data centers are trying to evade oversight by utility regulators by building their own private power plants. Excluding non-grid-connected power plants from acid rain requirements violates the Clean Air Act and has attracted the opposition of members of Congress as well as environmental organizations. Earthjustice wrote to EPA to oppose the proposal as unlawful under the Clean Air Act.

Polluting places that already fail to meet air quality standards

In July, EPA issued a guidance document to allow AI data centers and other developers otherwise subject to New Source Review standards to delay obtaining legally required offsetting emission reductions until the plant is operating, instead of at the time of permitting. The guidance would limit communities’ ability to oppose projects that threaten their air quality and health. This new guidance violates Clean Air Act requirements that enforceable offsetting reductions be secured before issuance of construction permits. The guidance also departs from EPA’s past practice, which acknowledged the difficulty in enforcing the offset requirement after a plant is constructed.

For example, Earthjustice opposes the use of offset credits for a more than 4GW gas-fired power plant being built to serve an Amazon AI data center on the location of a former coal plant in Homer City, Pennsylvania. Earthjustice objected to emissions credits where Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection had failed to identify the source of emission reductions for a gas-fired power plant that emit over 300 tons of smog-causing volatile organic compounds a year. Under the administration’s new proposal, communities would effectively be blocked from fighting offsets at these and other kinds of industrial projects before they begin operating.

Starting construction without permits

In May, EPA proposed a rule to allow data centers, power plants, and other industrial facilities to begin construction work before obtaining required air permits. New facilities that would be major sources of air pollution must go through an extensive process to review their emissions and pollution controls; to consider alternatives as well as the costs and benefits of the project; to allow for public participation; and to ensure protection of air quality for nearby and downwind residents. Earthjustice and many other environmental and public health groups filed detailed comments opposing the proposal to accelerate the siting of data centers and power plants that would have a range of harmful environmental and public health effects. EPA has yet to issue a final rule and response to comments.

The administration seeks to promote the rapid buildout of data centers across the United States and pledges to expedite permitting for AI data centers by weakening Clean Air Act regulations, promising to “identify, revise, or repeal regulations, rules, memoranda, administrative orders, guidance documents, policy statements, and interagency agreements that unnecessarily hinder AI development or deployment.”

Everyone deserves clean air and has a right to know about plans to increase harmful industrial pollution in their community. Instead, the EPA continues to abandon its mandate to protect our health, instead offering handouts to industrial polluters and AI data centers. Earthjustice will continue to fight these efforts to erode our rights and our environmental laws.

text:
The global mandate for Nature-based Solutions (NbS) to accelerate climate action has never been stronger — yet the countries that need these solutions most face the greatest barriers to implementing them. Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), particularly those in Sub-Saharan Africa, often lack the financial resources, institutional capacity, and technical expertise to turn NbS ambition into action.

This project, funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Denmark (Danida) and implemented through the ENACT Partnership and IUCN, directly addresses this gap. Running from 2025 to 2030, it supports ODA-eligible Sub-Saharan African countries in accelerating the adoption and implementation of NbS for climate adaptation — placing nature at the heart of resilient, inclusive development.

Objective

The project's central objective is to support ODA-eligible countries in Sub-Saharan Africa in accelerating the implementation and ambition of NbS within the context of sustainable and inclusive development for climate resilience. It aligns with and contributes to the ENACT Partnership Operational Roadmap 2025–2030, with NbS for Adaptation and Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) as a central pillar of climate transformation.

Specifically, the project aims to:

Influence international policy and support national implementation for NbS for transformational adaptation in the implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs), aligned with National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs) and the Sustainable Development Goals;

Accelerate NbS and EbA implementation with climate-proofing outcomes;

Increase NbS ambition in policy and regulatory frameworks;

Strengthen governance and mobilise climate finance for NbS for adaptation; and

Mainstream NbS for adaptation into development plans and budgets, consistent with the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) and climate-resilient SDGs.

Theory of Change

The project's Theory of Change holds that if ODA-eligible countries are supported in accelerating NbS for climate action and resilience — through strengthened capacity, knowledge, and skills, and raised ambitions for gender equality, social development, and biodiversity outcomes — then the enabling environment for leadership, coordination, and climate finance mobilisation will be reinforced. This will mainstream climate action into wider development plans and budgets, leading to the increased adoption and implementation of NbS for adaptation and EbA as a central pillar of transformative climate-biodiversity action and sustainable development.

Technical support to report on EbA progress, aligned with global indicators and integrated into national reportingProduction of tailored country briefs and best practice case studies showcasing successful national NbS implementation;

Hosting national roundtables to advance policy actionIn-country support for the implementation and finance of transformational adaptation across NDCs/NAPs/LT-LEDs

The NAbSA Framework

A cornerstone of the project's implementation approach is the NAbSA Operational Framework — a co-designed, practitioner-focused decision-making support system that equips implementers and decision-makers with the data and tools needed to make informed, inclusive, and sustainable choices. Built on learning from over 150 organisations across 30 countries, the NAbSA dashboard integrates AI-supported analytics to assess action options, estimate costs, and quantify economic impact. The project will pilot-test this dashboard in partner countries, linking it to ENACT's global goals tracking and IUCN's NbS Navigator platform.

Expected Outcomes

Partner countries supported through this project will be positioned to:

Mainstream NbS for adaptation and resilience in NDC 3.0, NAPs, and Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) implementation and investment plans, aligned with the NAbSA Operational Framework;

Enhance interinstitutional coordination to catalyse the implementation of transformative NbS policies for adaptation and resilience;

Mobilise public and private finance for NbS to support adaptation and resilience;

Receive guided support in implementing NbS for adaptation with climate and development outcomes across priority subsectors; and

Become global leaders on NbS — influencing international policy across the Rio Conventions and building partnerships with country peers across regions.

ENACT's Broader Vision

This project contributes to ENACT's overarching goals of protecting the resilience of at least 1 billion vulnerable people (including 500 million women and girls), securing up to 2.4 billion hectares of ecosystem integrity, and significantly increasing global nature-based mitigation efforts through the protection, conservation, and restoration of carbon-rich ecosystems.

text:
During the spring 2026 semester, I taught Climate Change Law and Policy at the Indiana University McKinney School of Law. The last time I taught the class was in 2021 before I joined the Biden Administration. Boy, how times have changed! Because of actions by the current Administration attempting to dismantle EPA’s regulatory authority over greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act, including most notably the rescission of the Endangerment Finding, a course that in 2021 required six hours on EPA climate programs required less than half that amount in 2026. I expect I will have more work to do in future years, depending on how the legal challenges to these actions are decided.

To prepare for the course, I found myself having to learn new material (imagine!). In particular, I focused on the citizen climate suits, especially Juliana v. United States [see Juliana v. United States, 947 F.3d 1159, 1171 (9th Cir. 2020)], and the numerous efforts by state and local governments to seek damages from the fossil fuel industry through litigation or state legislation.

My students and I were inspired by the energy and creativity of the States of Hawaii, Connecticut, Vermont, and New York, the cities of New York and Honolulu, and others, struggling to plan and pay for infrastructure and other solutions to protect their residents, institutions, and businesses from flooding, wildfires, sea level rise, extreme heat, and extreme weather—the increasing impacts of our changing climate. But we were also worn down by their continuous court losses. Industry defendants have successfully argued that the Compact Clause, federal pre-emption, the Dormant Commerce Clause, political questions, and the Supremacy Clause preclude states and local governments from bringing tort claims such as nuisance, trespass, or misrepresentation, or constitutional claims under the public trust doctrine. While increasingly acknowledging the undeniability of harm from climate change caused by emissions of greenhouse gases, courts have mostly thrown up their hands at finding a path to give plaintiffs their day in court.

text:
Colorado air-quality regulators approved a third and final set of rules Friday to reduce methane emissions released in oil and gas production, becoming the first state to draw up regulations based on two-year-old U.S. Environmental Protection Agency guidelines.

State leaders considered and passed the rules in three phases over the past 19 months. In February 2025, the Colorado Air Quality Control Commission established a timeline to phase out natural-gas-driven compressors and pumps by 2029. Then, earlier this year, commissioners created a crosswalk between federal requirements and Colorado’s decade-old methane regulations that helped to inform producers on how to meet the federal standard.

Finally, during a three-day hearing this week, the AQCC firmed up rules around the monitoring and reporting on pieces of equipment at existing oil-and-gas facilities that are meant to control emissions. These including things such as closed venting systems, covers and enclosed combustion devices at locations such as well sites, storage-vessel facilities and natural-gas-processing facilities.

An economic impact analysis indicated that state leaders don’t expect emissions reductions directly from what are known as the “Quad OC” rules — referring to the subpart of federal law to which they conform — but that is misleading in some sense. While the new regulations aren’t expected to lower methane emissions on their own, they will go a long way toward preventing fugitive emissions escaping from processing equipment, which several supporters said can be a significant source of air pollution.

How the rules will limit methane emissions

“What we’re doing here is really protecting public health and the environment,” AQCC member Martha Rudolph said near the end of the rulemaking hearing. “We hear that (as a request) from community members frequently, and we acknowledge that. But I really want to acknowledge that today.”

Part of Colorado’s eight-year push to cut emissions from industries ranging from oil and gas to commercial buildings to manufacturing, the Quad OC rules did not generate the same industry pushback and warnings of economic infeasibility as some other regulations have. However, leaders of the oil-and-gas industry warned that they will not come without costs to companies already dealing with a significant uptick in regulatory overhead that has contributed to a significant decrease in the number of oil and gas rigs operating in the state.

Companies operating the regulated equipment will, for example, have to inspect the equipment more frequently for leaks and repair malfunctions more quickly when they discover them. Oil companies extracting natural gas with a high amount of methane from oil wells will have to capture that gas rather than burning it off.

The heaviest debate during the hearing centered on a Colorado Air Pollution Control Division proposal that operators of enclosed combustion devices designed to burn up at least 95% of potentially harmful emissions that enter them must monitor these devices more frequently. Rather than record the minimum and maximum flow through the devices and report that on an annual basis, operators must continuously monitor the flow of gases through the machinery and ensure they are moving at a proper speed to maximize destruction of volatile organic compounds and hazardous air pollutants.

Costs to smaller oil-and-gas producers

Such a requirement will not be cheap, industry leaders said. Just five years after new regulations required ECD operators to procure flow meters for more frequent monitoring, this provision likely will cause the same companies to have to upgrade them or to buy actuators to ensure a more consistent flow for maximum pollutant destruction. And the new rules will require this not just for equipment falling under EPA’s Quad OC guidelines but for a wider range of equipment under the state’s Regulation 7 guidelines pertaining to lower-emitting and smaller-scale activities.

Clay Taylor — an attorney for Williams Weese Pepple & Ferguson representing petroleum-industry groups — estimated this expansion of the regulations will pull in thousands of other ECDs, as every controlled storage tank in Colorado has at least one. Not only will such retrofits be pricey, but the originally proposed compliance deadline of April 1 would have meant that tanks in remote locations on the Western Slope and elsewhere would have required the work in the dead of winter, likely slowing installations.

Colorado Oil & Gas Association Vice President of Regulatory Affairs Ryan Steadley noted that the economic impact analysis that APCD performed on the rules did not signal a cost estimate to operators for this work that most definitely will consume resources, which he said could create “significant legal vulnerability for the rule.” And both he and Taylor questioned the efficacy of the requirement when the same EIA estimated no reduction in emissions from the rule — an opinion shared by several members of the AQCC.

A “common-sense” practice?

Yet environmental groups from GreenLatinos to Environmental Defense Fund to Physicians for Social Responsibility specifically asked commissioners to expand the rule beyond just Quad OC-covered equipment, calling it key to preventing fugitive emissions. And staffers like Jeremy Schuster of APCD’s planning and policy program said that he asked industry leaders repeatedly how much such retrofitting would cost but could not get an answer.

AQCC member Curtis Reuter proposed a delay in the start of the new regulations for non-Quad OC facilities until the start of 2030, saying that would give time to save up and plan for upgrades and would allow APCD staff more than just eight months to consider requests for alternative monitoring arrangements, which are allowed under the rules. But fellow commissioner Jana Milford countered with a proposal to extend the deadlines for non-Quad-OC equipment operators only by one year, until April 2028, and her suggestion won out in a 5-4 vote of commissioners.

“I think it’s just common-sense, good engineering practice that you’re going to operate and maintain control over devices like these,” Milford explained.

Reduction in methane emissions expected

Many of Colorado’s larger oil and gas producers, which are all subject to Quad OC regulations, offered little pushback to the rules other than clarifying several of the provisions. Reuter applauded industry and environmental groups and APCD officials for reaching “a remarkable consensus through this process.”

Environmental groups lauded the final vote, saying that such steps to capture and reduce emissions are desperately needed as Colorado remains in severe nonattainment of EPA ozone standards, leading to many days this summer that triggered struggles for asthmatics and other northern Front Range residents with cardiovascular conditions.

“Thankfully, solutions are available, and with today’s vote our state leaders have taken another step toward making our air safe to breathe,” said Kirsten Schatz, clean air advocate for the CoPIRG Foundation, in a news release after the final vote. “Especially when better, cleaner technology is available, we should no longer tolerate preventable releases of harmful pollution into our air.”

text:
A new aluminum coating could simplify how battery components are manufactured by protecting the metal during forming while adding properties needed inside electric vehicle and energy storage systems.

Novelis is expanding its portfolio of coated aluminum solutions for battery applications, targeting components including battery enclosures, casings and electrical connectors known as bus bars.

The approach combines automotive-grade aluminum sheet with surface treatments designed to improve corrosion resistance and formability. The company says the coated material can also be engineered to provide electrical insulation for specific battery applications.

A key part of the technology is a water-based coating applied to aluminum coils before they are formed into components. The coating is designed to remain effective after stamping, potentially allowing manufacturers to remove some processing steps used with untreated aluminum.

Coating simplifies battery production

Battery components must withstand demanding manufacturing and operating conditions. Aluminum is attractive because it is lightweight, durable and recyclable, but components may require additional surface treatments to protect them from corrosion or provide electrical insulation.

Novelis says its pre-applied coating can address some of those requirements before the aluminum reaches the forming stage. Because the coating is already on the coil, manufacturers may be able to reduce reliance on external lubrication and additional e-coating processes.

“Leveraging decades of automotive expertise, we have developed aluminum solutions that combine advanced surface technologies with high-performance sheet products for demanding battery applications,” says Milan Felberbaum, Director R&D, Novelis Europe. “By integrating these capabilities, we help customers improve manufacturing efficiency while supporting battery performance and durability.”

More from Energy

See All

The company says the coating has already been proven and is in use on its advanced coating line in Germany. Its ability to withstand stamping is important because battery components often need to be shaped into complex forms after the coating is applied.

Aluminum targets tougher battery demands

The coated aluminum can be used for battery enclosures and casings, where corrosion protection can help improve component durability. It can also be tailored for electrical insulation, a property that can be useful for components that need to prevent unwanted electrical contact.

The technology is aimed at both electric mobility and stationary energy storage. That gives the material a role across different battery systems rather than limiting it to automotive applications.

Novelis is also emphasizing the use of recycled aluminum. The company says high-recycled-content, low-carbon aluminum can support efforts to reduce the environmental impact of battery supply chains. Closed-loop recycling could allow aluminum recovered from products to be returned to the manufacturing cycle.

The announcement is therefore focused less on changing battery chemistry and more on changing the material and manufacturing process around the battery. By combining aluminum’s low weight with a pre-applied coating, the company is targeting a way to make battery components easier to manufacture while meeting durability and insulation requirements.

Fewer steps for battery makers

The approach could also help manufacturers reduce manufacturing complexity if fewer coating and lubrication stages are required. However, the announcement does not provide quantified figures for cost savings, production-time reductions or improvements in battery performance.

Novelis is positioning the expanded portfolio for the growing battery and energy storage markets, building on its experience supplying aluminum products to the automotive industry.

text:
Republican regulators on Friday threw a wrench in Amazon's plan to power a $10 billion data center project in North Carolina — citing President Donald Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

The GOP-controlled North Carolina Utilities Commission rejected a half-billion-dollar natural gas project sought by Duke Energy, the state's largest utility, to primarily serve a 21-building Amazon facility under construction near Charlotte.

Republican commissioners on the five-member panel said Duke did not adequately demonstrate how consumers would be shielded from paying for the peaker plant. GOP members William Brawley, Tommy Tucker and Donald van der Vaart said Duke failed to explain how it would "adhere to its commitments under the Ratepayer Protection Pledge" — a voluntary agreement brokered by the White House.

The denial comes amid the growing backlash to data centers and artificial intelligence. And it underscores growing skepticism among state regulators towards energy projects designed to meet the facilities' massive electricity needs.

The 250-megawatt gas project in south-central North Carolina was slated for the existing Smith Energy Complex, home to five other units. The GOP commissioners said if Duke plans to reapply, the utility would need to offer cost recovery mechanisms that comply with the White House's voluntary agreement.

Duke Energy is one of hundreds of utilities that have signed Trump's pledge to ensure tech companies — not everyday customers — pay for the massive electricity and grid updates needed for AI data centers.

Duke spokesperson Craig Wilson said the utility was disappointed by the commission's decision and would assess next steps.

"We believe we have demonstrated that the [project] is part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina," Wilson said in an email.

A spokesperson for Amazon did not respond to a request for comment.

Of the two Democrats on the panel, one was not present and the other dissented on procedural grounds.

Commissioner Floyd McKissick took issue with his colleagues basing their decision on who would pay for the project — a reference to the invocation of Trump's ratepayer protection pledge, which is not legally binding.

The commission's rejection Friday is not permanent, and Duke will have a chance to refile its application. In the meantime, Amazon secured permits from the state's Department of Environmental Quality to run 57 temporary non-emergency diesel generators for a year while the hyperscale facility connects to the electric grid.

Amazon broke ground on the project last year. The 21-building campus is slated for completion in 2029 or 2030.

In addition to the non-emergency generators, Amazon secured a second permit to run nearly 600 diesel-fired backup generators.

The permits have drawn opposition from the local community in Hamlet, a small town in Richmond County, which already contends with industrial air pollution from other energy projects. During a heated hearing in July attended by nearly 200 people, residents expressed concern over new emissions of fine particulate matter, which is linked to cancer.

"Amazon, one of the wealthiest companies in the world, and Duke Energy, a regulated monopoly, can and should do better than belching deadly soot pollution into the air North Carolinians breathe from a whopping 649 diesel-fired generators powering a massive data center," Caroline Cress, senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center, said in a statement.

Commission staff could recall only one other time over the past 35 years that the commission had rejected a Duke natural gas project, said Lucy Edmondson, chief counsel for the commission's public staff, which represents ratepayers before the panel. A decade ago, the panel greenlit two combined-cycle gas plants but denied a third combustion turbine.

The Republican commissioners also took issue with approving new gas generation before approving Duke's long-range energy plan, slated for this winter. They likewise said Duke failed to evaluate reasonable alternatives to the plant.

Commissioner van der Vaart, who previously has voiced opposition to solar energy, said Duke had not considered whether a battery storage project would meet power needs more cheaply.

Tucker, another Republican commissioner, said he worried the price tag was too high for a plant that ultimately may not be needed.

"Given the size of this expenditure and the associated possibility for stranded assets, I believe that the Commission requires more evidence supporting the need for the Proposed Facility," he wrote.

Will Scott, the Environmental Defense Fund's North Carolina policy director, said he's never seen the commission deny a project before with that kind of "strong language" about not creating a stranded asset.

"It's very rare for one of these to be denied," he said.

Scott noted the commission is in the process of putting a large load tariff in place, which would clearly assign data centers' energy costs to the operators. But as it stands, the costs of this gas project would be borne by ratepayers.

name: EVs
title: China's Overcapacity Could Also Be An Energy Solution - OpEd - Eurasia Review
authors: Azhar Azam, Dr. Mohamed Chtatou, Seif A. Harrasy, Diálogo Américas
description:
In 2025, China’s electricity demand rose about 5%.
Clean power expanded fast enough to meet that surge, pushing thermal generation, mostly coal-based, down 0.7% — the first annual decline in a decade, according to Ember’s China Energy Transition Review 2026.
Even so, clean technologies are beginning to change China’s energy ecosystem.
China’s clean-tech overcapacity has become an essential feature of the global energy transition.
Beijing’s role in the global energy transition is unlikely to diminish in the near term.
text:
Key Takeaways:

Ember’s China Energy Transition Review 2026: 2025 power demand +~5%; clean generation covered the rise and thermal (mostly coal) fell 0.7%—first annual drop in a decade (unlike 2015, when thermal fell because demand barely grew). EVs cut ~0.4–0.5 mb/d of gasoline; broader avoided oil ~1 mb/d or more—above OECD Europe’s 179 million barrels of government strategic stocks at end-2025. Coal generation has been roughly flat on a 12-month average since early 2024.

Scale at home: ~1,700 GW of wind and solar added in a decade (more than the whole 2015 grid); 2025 battery storage +84%, China ~60% of new global storage; electric trucks ~26% of new sales. H1 2025 curtailment: solar 5.7%, wind 6.6%; Tibet, Xinjiang, Qinghai above the 10% cap. 1 Sept 2026: consumption tax on mainstream batteries; solar-cell levy due 2027. Global clean-tech trade ~$479bn in 2025.

U.S. and EU treat surplus panels, batteries, and EVs as industrial risk; the same surplus cut prices and pushed kit into developing markets (Ethiopia EVs, Pakistan solar) after tariffs redirected flows. EU still leans on Chinese panels and batteries; U.S. IRA does not fix upstream minerals (CSIS). India added 37 GW of solar in 2025 vs China’s 315.1 GW. Author: use the cheap kit without deepening lock-in.

In 2025, China’s electricity demand rose about 5%. Clean power expanded fast enough to meet that surge, pushing thermal generation, mostly coal-based, down 0.7% — the first annual decline in a decade, according to Ember’s China Energy Transition Review 2026. This marked a significant departure from 2015, when thermal generation fell largely because electricity demand barely grew, rising just 0.5%, the slowest pace since 1974.

Beyond electricity, rapid transport electrification is also reducing domestic oil demand. Ember notes that electric vehicles (EVs) are displacing around 0.4–0.5 million barrels of gasoline a day, while broader estimates put avoided oil demand at around or above 1 million barrels a day — roughly 365–400 million barrels a year. That is more than double the 179 million barrels of government-held strategic oil inventories in OECD Europe at the end of 2025.

The findings complicate a debate usually framed as a purely industrial problem. The United States and European Union (EU) see Beijing’s dominance in solar panels, batteries and EVs as a source of economic and strategic vulnerability — manufacturing capacity built on a scale that domestic demand alone can’t absorb, leaving foreign markets to take the surplus.

Yet the overcapacity triggering these concerns is also accelerating the global clean-energy transition by making these technologies cheaper and more widely available, as reflected in global trade of clean-tech products that reached an estimated $479 billion in 2025.

Much of this trade has been driven by China’s production. In sectors such as EVs, Beijing’s manufacturing has outstripped domestic demand, putting downward pressure on global prices. These cost declines have, in turn, supported faster electrification around the world.

China’s manufacturing surplus shouldn’t be viewed in isolation. The same manufacturing capacity that has created excess supply is also supporting a rapidly expanding domestic clean-energy market. Over the past decade, China has added almost 1,700 gigawatts of wind and solar capacity — more than its entire power system in 2015. In 2025, battery-storage installations grew 84%, with China accounting for roughly 60% of new storage deployed worldwide. Electric trucks reached about 26% of new sales, a share leading European economies have just achieved in passenger cars.

Deployment at such a scale doesn’t mean all that capacity is being fully absorbed. In the first half of 2025, China’s solar curtailment rate rose to 5.7% and wind curtailment to 6.6%, with curtailment in western regions such as Tibet, Xinjiang and Qinghai exceeding the country’s 10% tolerance, according to national grid data. Grid bottlenecks and limited local demand have made it difficult to fully use some of the electricity generated by new renewable capacity.

Even so, clean technologies are beginning to change China’s energy ecosystem. Ember finds that coal generation has been broadly flat on a 12-month moving average since early 2024. It marks an important shift: China’s clean-energy buildout is quickly displacing fossil-fuel generation.

Beijing is now responding to the industrial complaints created by overcapacity. On September 1, a new consumption tax on mainstream batteries took effect, with equivalent levies on solar cells due in 2027. These tax policies may help to weed out inefficient capacity, force the exit of low-tier players and ease international trade tensions arising from overproduction.

Meanwhile, the impact of falling costs is reciprocated in affordability — one of the main constraints on decarbonization. For many emerging and developing economies, limited fiscal space is the major barrier to energy transition. As prices drop, lower-cost imports have expanded their access to clean technologies.

Trade restrictions have had limited effect. Rather than curbing China’s clean-energy exports, tariffs and industrial-policy tools introduced by the United States and EU have redirected a growing share of trade flows toward developing markets. From EVs in Ethiopia to discounted solar panels in Pakistan, China’s industrial scale has lowered costs across many developing economies, contributing to global emissions reductions.

As clean-energy investment expands, China’s dominance is perceived differently across regions. Many developing economies view it as an opportunity to gain access to clean technologies at lower costs; advanced economies associate Beijing’s scale with industrial overcapacity.

For instance, solar deployment in the EU has grown strongly in recent years, but the bloc still relies heavily on China for solar panels and key upstream inputs. The same pattern is emerging in EV batteries: EU efforts to restructure and localize production have eased some overcapacity risks while also increasing reliance on Chinese battery suppliers.

This creates a policy trade-off for Europe — greater industrial autonomy would strengthen long-term supply-chain resilience but is likely to raise costs and slow the pace of decarbonization, while continued reliance sustains faster deployment but leaves Europe exposed to ongoing dependencies.

The United States faces a similar challenge. Despite tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act, China accounts for the majority of global clean-tech manufacturing capacity. Washington is scaling deployment in areas such as battery storage, emerging as second to Beijing, but as CSIS analysis highlights, expansion in downstream segments does not resolve upstream constraints such as limited domestic reserves and critical mineral processing capacity, limiting the scope of full self-sufficiency.

India follows a different but related trajectory. Its renewable energy installed capacity has expanded quickly, but the scale gap with China is substantial: Beijing added 315.1 gigawatts (GW) of solar capacity in 2025 versus New Delhi’s 37 GW.

China’s clean-tech overcapacity has become an essential feature of the global energy transition. While criticized as trade distortion, it has contributed to significant cost reductions in solar, battery and EV technologies, accelerating their adoption across developing, emerging and advanced economies. Yet the same concentration that drives lower costs also generates structural vulnerabilities, increasing exposure of importing economies to supply-chain disruption, geopolitical friction and industrial dependence — as reflected in policy responses from Brussels and Washington.

China’s excess manufacturing capacity and rapid domestic deployment actually are mutually reinforcing. Producing more solar panels, batteries and EVs has intensified competition and pushed prices down. Those lower prices have made it easier to deploy the same technologies at home and abroad. China’s manufacturing scale is therefore doing two things at once: creating concerns about excess capacity while also making clean technologies cheap enough to expand rapidly, including inside China’s own energy system.

Beijing’s role in the global energy transition is unlikely to diminish in the near term. For policymakers around the world, the challenge is not just to reduce reliance on Chinese clean technologies, but to harness the benefits of Beijing’s scale to strengthen energy security and accelerate electrification without deepening strategic dependencies.

text:
The NEPA order (see 2609080062) would codify the statutory definition of "major federal action" (MFA) in the FCC's rules and make it clear that NEPA requirements apply only to such actions. Under the order, space-based operations and earth station deployments wouldn't constitute MFAs. Space operations are by definition extraterritorial and thus fall among the exclusions to NEPA’s definition of an MFA, the draft order says.

The draft also says spectrum authorizations for space-based operations don’t equate to federal oversight and control of nonfederal deployments in space. U.S. jurisdiction in space “extends only to territories where the United States is sovereign and the United States is not legally sovereign over outer space, as other nations are free to enter and operate there, including operations the United States disapproves of.”

Ian Christensen, senior director of private-sector programs for the Secure World Foundation, said in an email that the FCC's assertion that satellites are exempt from NEPA "is not a new policy." It's simply a policy signal "in line with the overall approach of streamlining and regulatory reduction that the current FCC has adopted."

Multiple environmental groups agreed that the draft order would clearly codify what's been FCC practice for a while.

The item represents "a HUGE victory," emailed Jim Dunstan, general counsel for TechFreedom, which has previously argued that NEPA doesn't apply to space (see 2109280053). The commission "has dodged the question multiple times and has finally come out and said it plainly," he said.

While the agency has long said that space activity is subject to a categorical exclusion under NEPA, "there's a huge difference" between that and saying space activity isn't an MFA under NEPA, Dunstan added. A categorical exclusion can be overcome if the FCC determines that the action might have a significant environmental impact, meaning any licensing action could be appealed with arguments that the agency ignored evidence of such an impact, he said.

But by declaring that satellite licensing is not an MFA, the FCC doesn't even need to consider evidence of environmental impact at the licensing stage, he noted.

Dunstan also said the FCC action will surely be challenged in a court, which could force an ultimate ruling on the fundamental question.

Frank said the FCC move is unsurprising. Going forward, parties will still be able to petition the FCC to challenge space system approvals on environmental grounds, she said, and Congress could also act to define what sort of review is needed for these sorts of projects. However, she added, she's not aware of any legislation that gets at the topic.

"It is becoming increasingly clear that we need a new regulatory environment to match the ambition, and plans, of the space sector," DarkSky International CEO Ruskin Hartley said in an email. "Ultimately, it is up to Congress to act on that in a way that protects things the American public values, like clean air, clean water, and dark skies."

title: Court Strikes Down Trump's EPA Cancellation of $7B Solar for All Program
description:
Nationwide, Solar for All is expected to save an estimated $350 million annually on energy bills and generate 200,000 new jobs.
“Solar for All was built to open that door, and EPA tried to slam it shut.
“Electricity bills are skyrocketing, so low-cost solar projects — which guarantee big savings — are needed now more than ever.
Today’s decision makes clear that EPA unlawfully terminated the Solar for All Program,” said Jillian Blanchard, Senior Vice President of Climate Change and Environmental Justice at L4GG.

text:
Nationwide, Solar for All is expected to save an estimated $350 million annually on energy bills and generate 200,000 new jobs. Photo: Shutterstock

September 18, 2026 (Boston, MA) – A federal judge has ruled that the Environmental Protection Agency unlawfully canceled the $7 billion Solar for All program, striking down the agency’s decision to end a nationwide program designed to lower electricity bills and bring affordable solar power to families and communities across the country.

“Clean, affordable power like solar shouldn’t be a closed-door luxury,” said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at Conservation Law Foundation (CLF). “Solar for All was built to open that door, and EPA tried to slam it shut. Today’s ruling pushes it back open. Communities have waited long enough. Nearly every family is looking for ways to cut their energy bill. These dollars should go where Congress intended: toward lower energy bills, less climate pollution, good jobs, and cleaner air.”

“The court ruled the Trump Administration never should have terminated Solar for All because Congress intended it to continue, and EPA broke the law when it killed the program and pocketed the money,” said Southern Environmental Law Center Senior Attorney Nick Torrey. “Electricity bills are skyrocketing, so low-cost solar projects — which guarantee big savings — are needed now more than ever. Today’s victory means EPA must stop sitting on the $7 billion in funding for this program and start getting it out into communities to provide hardworking American families much-needed relief.”

“Today’s ruling confirms what we have argued from the beginning: EPA cannot erase a $7 billion program that Congress created and funded. For more than a year, families and communities have seen higher energy bills while billions of dollars intended to lower electricity costs sat out of reach. Today’s decision makes clear that EPA unlawfully terminated the Solar for All Program,” said Jillian Blanchard, Senior Vice President of Climate Change and Environmental Justice at L4GG.

In 2024, the EPA awarded $7 billion for “Solar for All,” estimating the program would reach more than 900,000 households, save families $350 million a year on electricity bills, and support 200,000 jobs and workforce training opportunities.

In August 2025, the Trump administration abruptly canceled the program before much of that funding could reach communities. CLF, the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC), Lawyers for Good Government (L4GG), and the Lawyers Committee for Rhode Island, filed the lawsuit last October on behalf of workers, businesses, nonprofits, and individuals harmed by EPA’s cancellation. Plaintiffs include the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, Rhode Island Center for Justice, Solar United Neighbors, an individual homeowner, and solar businesses.

text:
Mission Solar Energy’s solar panel manufacturing site in San Antonio, Texas, considered one of the longest-running panel assembly operations in the United States, may soon receive a boost from a global manufacturer.

Mission Solar has been making solar panels in the United States since 2014 and is owned by OCI Company, a South Korean chemical conglomerate that is involved with solar project development and polysilicon production. OCI started the assembler to supply panels to its own utility-scale projects in Texas. Mission Solar has since worked through solar panel distribution channels and mostly supplied the U.S. residential sector but was attempting plays into larger markets. The company is currently listed as having a 500-MW annual module assembly capacity in San Antonio.

Sam Martens, president of Mission Solar, submitted testimony in the ongoing antidumping/countervailing duty (AD/CVD) investigation into solar cell imports from India, Indonesia and Laos. In addition to reiterating to the U.S. International Trade Commission the challenges the U.S. solar industry faces from unfairly priced imports, Martens commented on Mission Solar’s Texas factory.

“Despite trying our best to be cost-competitive, our customers repeatedly told us that our prices are too high. Subject producers have even offered prices well below our cost of production. We simply cannot cut prices that far, and we often ended up losing the sale instead,” he said. “The continual loss of sales and revenue forced us to curtail our production, leaving us with significant excess capacity.

“Lower utilization has naturally resulted in reduced shifts and reduced employees,” Martens continued. “For example, we previously employed more than 200 workers. But, due to the market conditions caused by subject imports, we only had 70 employees by 2025, and have now temporarily ceased all manufacturing operations and related employment.

“If injurious subject imports remain unrestrained in the face of potentially shrinking demand, I am afraid that the domestic industry will once again face rising closures and mass layoffs,” he concluded.

There have been no layoff announcements by Mission Solar in Texas worker adjustment and retraining notification notices, so if employment has been temporarily ceased, it’s likely to have resulted in furloughs. When asked, Mission Solar representatives were unable to comment on the matter to Solar Power World.

It’s an unfortunate trend for long-established U.S. solar panel manufacturers. Silfab Solar furloughed workers in August at its South Carolina manufacturing site due to “temporary constraints affecting the availability of certain materials required for production.” Heliene laid off nearly 100 workers in August at its Minnesota solar panel assembly facility due to “unforeseen business circumstances.” Qcells furloughed 1,000 employees at its Georgia operations last year, but was able resume production four months later.

Mission Solar, which has long operated a small-output solar panel factory at a mixed-use community located on the former Brooks Air Force Base, announced in 2022 it would expand operations to reach 1 GW of annual module manufacturing capacity. The company built a 200,000-sq-ft addition on its property, but it was instead later described as a warehouse.

The warehouse was then assumed to become the starting point of Mission and OCI’s solar cell manufacturing operations, which the two companies announced in 2025. They would invest $265 million into the site to eventually reach 2 GW of annual cell manufacturing capacity. Martens confirmed in his ITC testimony that actual construction plans never progressed further.

That warehouse is back in play after a filing with the Texas Dept. of Licensing and Regulation in August. The filing says that $15 million will be spent to renovate the existing warehouse into the “Elite Solar factory [f]or manufacturing.” Construction is expected to begin in October and be completed in June 2027.

Elite Solar, a Singapore-headquartered panel brand (previously known as ET Solar), has affiliated panel manufacturing operations across the globe. The company’s flagship sites are now based in Egypt and Indonesia, but it has a longstanding relationship with OCI and is jointly developing a solar wafer production facility in Vietnam. This partnership could be extending to panel manufacturing in Texas.

Elite Solar provided no comment when asked by Solar Power World about the San Antonio factory plans.

description:
Data Centers have been reshaping communities.
Until today, that has been our path with data centers.
Across the country Republicans are attempting to kill clean energy and hand out massive giveaways to their Big Polluter billionaire donors.
The ads focused on how the Republican incumbent voted to cut clean energy driving up utility bills so the wealthy could get another cut.
Lawmakers must also address the significant concerns communities have about data centers’ impact on water, air, climate, and noise pollution.
text:
Your weekly resource to learn what the environmental movement is saying about the news of the day and the political fight of our generation. This week, we’re covering who’s responsibly (and irresponsibly) offering solutions to data center development, energy affordability, and air and water pollution.

Be sure to follow LCV on Facebook, Instagram, BlueSky, and TikTok.

QUOTES OF THE WEEK:

“In the past two years, I’ve watched and fought back with an angry fire in my heart as Trump’s reckless EPA leaders have advanced costly and harmful rollbacks to protections for our communities, our air, water, and land, all for the primary benefit of oil, gas, and coal CEOs.”

— Matthew Davis, LCV vice president of federal policy and former EPA scientist, during a press event where congressional Democrats introduced a bill to restore EPA’s mission of protecting the environment and public health.

“We need real solutions to rising costs of energy, like the Energy Bills Relief Act, rather than backroom deals that help to shield big polluters and data centers while doing very little to address the affordability crisis that people are facing.”

— Rep. Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) on the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that falls short of protecting ratepayers from skyrocketing energy costs and will have little practical impact on lowering bills.

“The Trump administration is spending nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds to cancel 12 offshore wind leases at the same time when Americans’ utility bills are rising. Their priorities are completely out of whack.”

— Rep. Chellie Pingree (ME-01) at a press conference calling out Trump’s corrupt offshore wind buyouts.

TOP NEWS IN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY

STATE NEWS

SPANBERGER DATA CENTER PLAN: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger announced her plan to enact new datacenter guardrails for the Commonwealth. Her data center accountability framework bans non-disclosure agreements for data centers, accelerates clean energy deployment and makes it easier for data centers to bring their own clean power, sets water usage and noise regulations, helps ensure data centers pay for their fair share of electric transmission and generation costs, and limits new gas energy generation.

VALCV TAKE: Virginia League of Conservation Voters Executive Director Michael Town spoke at the governor’s press conference today, saying, “You can’t go too many places in America today where people are not raising concerns about data centers. For us in Virginia, this is old news. Data Centers have been reshaping communities. Our electric bills keep going up. Neighborhoods have black clouds over them coming from diesel generators on the hottest days of the year. Local officials are cutting deals with companies and keeping the details secret from their voters. People are angry.”

“Virginians have been clamoring for action, and for the most part, their concerns have been falling on deaf ears. Virginia LCV represents voters from across the Commonwealth. We fight for a cleaner environment and for a healthier democracy. When the people are crying for help because their community is being polluted and no one is listening, both our environment and our democracy suffer. Until today, that has been our path with data centers. Today, that changes.“

“We and many of our partners are ready to work with Governor Spanberger as she leads Virginia into a new era of data center accountability. Together, we’ll cut pollution and we’ll protect communities. The path ahead will not be easy, and we will not always agree. Tomorrow the work begins. Today, we say thank you, Governor Spanberger, thank you for your commitment to tackle this issue and we stand ready to join you as we build a stronger, healthier and cleaner Virginia together.”

LCV TAKE: LCV President Pete Maysmith said, “People are fed up paying massive utility bills, watching Big Tech companies raise their rates to build new data centers that threaten more gas pollution in local communities’ clean air and water. This is why leadership matters. Governor Spanberger ran to address rising costs and today’s executive order and sweeping framework will help bring relief to Virginians and hold Big Tech accountable. We look forward to Gov. Spanberger working with Virginia LCV, other state partners, and the legislature to enact strong guardrails in the General Assembly. Across the country Republicans are attempting to kill clean energy and hand out massive giveaways to their Big Polluter billionaire donors. But the public is fighting back. We need more leaders like Abigail Spanberger who are ready to take on Big Tech and fight the source of rising energy costs.”

HAALAND DATA CENTER PLAN: Democratic candidate for New Mexico governor, Deb Haaland, announced her plan to establish a temporary moratorium on data centers on day one if elected. The pause would remain in effect until the state legislature enacts protections Haaland has called for, including clear standards for water use, clean energy, transparency and jobs associated with data centers.

CVNM ACTION FUND TAKE: On social media, Conservation Voters New Mexico Action Fund said, “Deb Haaland announced she will take executive action on day 1 as governor to put a moratorium on data centers until the state passes strong environmental and community guardrails and protections. She has made it clear that NM is ready to lead.”

NATIONAL NEWS

LCVVF RELEASES NEW POLLING ON CLEAN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY: New testing conducted by Tavern Research from June to August of 2026 determined that LCV Victory Fund’s early house program ads that ran in VA-01, MI-04 and AZ-02 improved results for Democrats by leveraging clean energy affordability. The ads focused on how the Republican incumbent voted to cut clean energy driving up utility bills so the wealthy could get another cut. After the ads aired, the named ballot moved a net 4 points toward the Democrat in all three districts. Read more here.

MEMBERS OF CONGRESS AND ADVOCATES CALL OUT TRUMP’S OFFSHORE WIND BUYOUTS: LCV joined labor, environmental advocates, and members of Congress to denounce the Trump administration’s attacks on offshore wind. As energy bills continue to skyrocket, the administration has used nearly $4 billion taxpayer dollars to buy out leases for offshore wind and force companies to invest that money into methane gas export projects, further increasing household costs and air and climate pollution.

OUR TAKE: LCV Legislative Director David Shadburn said, “As if energy costs were not high enough, the Trump administration has spent almost four billion taxpayer dollars to keep our energy costs high by blocking affordable clean offshore wind energy. Trump is instead directing our tax dollars to new LNG export projects, shipping gas overseas and actually driving prices back home even higher, all while enriching Trump’s fossil fuel donors. We stand with clean energy leaders in Congress who are fighting to hold this administration to account and lower costs for working families.”

HOUSE PASSES WINDOW DRESSING ON DATA CENTERS: The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that, on its own, falls short of addressing concerns about data centers and skyrocketing energy costs. The bill encourages states to consider protecting ratepayers from data centers, but fails to establish or require states to establish meaningful standards to address high consumer costs and the environmental impacts of data center development.

OUR TAKE: Last week, ahead of the vote, LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “No Representative should feel like a vote for this bill solves the concerns people back home have with data centers. The public is looking for their elected officials to take on utility corruption and guarantee that Big Tech will pay the full costs of infrastructure for their data centers and build the clean, reliable grid we all need. Lawmakers must also address the significant concerns communities have about data centers’ impact on water, air, climate, and noise pollution. They are fed up with corrupt backroom deals that cut out communities and don’t want data centers powered by dirtier and more expensive gas, diesel, or coal.

“The job won’t be done until there are real, enforceable guardrails to ensure environmental and public health protections, meaningful community input and benefits for communities hosting these facilities, and until Big Tech — not the public – pays the full cost of electricity and water and broader infrastructure upgrades.”

CLIMATE ATTACKS FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND CONGRESS

TRUMP’S EPA REPEALS POLLUTION STANDARDS FOR POWER PLANTS: Trump’s EPA issued a final rule repealing climate pollution limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants. Rolling back these emissions standards will increase climate and other pollution, drive up our energy bills, and have disastrous consequences on public health… all to benefit Trump’s Big Polluter allies. In addition, EPA launched a proposal that would abdicate the agency’s responsibility to regulate greenhouse gas emissions altogether, which will be open for public comment through November 2nd.

OUR TAKE: Ahead of the final rule, LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “Instead of holding polluters accountable, Trump and EPA administrator Lee Zeldin are determined to give free passes to Big Polluters at the expense of the health, safety, and budgets of our communities. By erasing limits on climate pollution for coal and methane gas plants while Trump is continuing to rush through data centers powered by coal and gas, the EPA is putting all of us, our health and our economy at tremendous risk. In order to benefit their Big Oil and Coal CEO donors, our families will get sicker, our utility costs will continue to skyrocket, our air will be dirtier, and we will face more extreme weather. Instead of repealing standards that are designed to protect us and provide billions of dollars in benefits, Lee Zeldin and the EPA should be protecting our communities by strengthening standards to reduce climate pollution and drive down energy, health, and disaster costs.”

CONGRESS’ BIG OIL HANDOUT WEEK: This week, congressional Republicans pushed for even more handouts to fossil fuel companies, including the House narrowly passing two Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolutions, H.J. Res. 210 and H.J. Res. 213, both of which seek to remove maritime ship air pollution limits that lower fuel oil use and ensure Big Oil profits remain sky-high. Before skipping town, Senate Republican leadership may bring up S.J. Res 208 and S.J. Res 207, both of which would drive up families’ costs at the pump by blocking longstanding air pollution and efficiency standards for cars.

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “In the last week before they head out for an extended recess, House Republican leadership decided to use their limited time to push for more handouts to Big Polluters, instead of passing legislation that will make life better and less expensive for everyday people. Across the country, people on both sides of the aisle are fed up with high prices fueled by Trump’s war in Iran, and they understand that the corrupt oil and gas industry is taking advantage of this crisis to drive prices to record levels, at all of our expense. Over 70% of respondents in recent polling support a windfall profits tax to return money to families and crack down on Big Oil’s war profiteering.

“This week, congressional Republicans proved that, even with midterms on the line, they are willing to sacrifice the health and financial well-being of their constituents to benefit Big Polluters. Sadly, it appears the public has come to expect this: by a 30 point margin they think the Republican party cares more about oil and gas CEOs than working families, and separate polling showed Americans view Oil and Gas as the ‘most corrupt’ industry in the country. Instead of padding oil and gas CEOs’ pockets, Congress should focus on deploying immediate relief, clean energy, and grid improvements to make electricity more affordable for families, and hold billionaire utility, oil and gas, and tech companies accountable.”

ICYMI: STATE NEWS

ARIZONA YOUTH ARE TURNING CLIMATE EDUCATION INTO ACTION: Through Chispa Arizona’s Plantando Semillas program, young people are building their knowledge of climate and environmental justice while developing the skills to advocate for their communities. Their work toward the Seal of Climate Literacy offers a look at how the next generation of Arizona climate leaders is learning, organizing, and making their voices heard. See youth in action here.

ICYMI: NATIONAL NEWS

LCVVF AND CFFE PAC LAUNCH $3.7 MILLION PAID FIELD PROGRAM: The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy PAC (CFFE PAC) and LCV Victory Fund, along with state affiliates and partners, announced a combined $3.7 million investment in field organizing programs encompassing Senate, House, and gubernatorial races to knock over 300,000 doors in Michigan and Ohio. Read more about the program here.

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “We need leaders who will prioritize people over polluters. We are thrilled to be partnering with the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy to go door to door to meet voters where they are. Across the country we are facing an affordability crisis and voters need to know that there are candidates who have platforms and plans to actually lower costs, especially utility costs. Voters deserve better. They deserve leaders who will stand up to Big Polluters, advocate for their communities, and look for our health and safety.”

LCVVF LAUNCHES $2.6 MILLION AD BLITZ: LCV Victory Fund announced a $1.6 million ad campaign calling out Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson’s record of voting against clean water protections, and a $1 million campaign targeting Mike Lawler (NY-17) and Scott Perry (PA-10).

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “The folks back home are fed up with what these Republican Representatives have been doing in Washington to raise costs and roll back basic environmental protections. They’re helping us tell these stories because voters deserve to know why their utility costs have risen over the past year and corporate interests are put ahead of keeping families healthy and safe.”

LCVVF WEEKLY ROUNDUP: We are so back! With just 46 days until Election Day, LCV Victory Fund’s weekly report is back. Each week we will be sharing exclusives, new ads and organizing programing, paid media trackers, and the latest happenings on energy affordability this election season. Check out this week’s roundup here.

LCV, NRDC ACTION FUND LAUNCH PAID FIELD PROGRAM: LCV and NRDC Action Fund each launched a paid field canvassing program to work alongside campaigns in battleground states across the country. The LCV program, called the Clean Energy Corps, will run in three high-priority Congressional Districts and knock over 150,000 doors to mobilize voters in support of pro-environment, pro-democracy candidates, including Representative Kathy Castor (FL-14) and candidates Rebecca Bennett (NJ-07), and Paige Cognetti (PA-08).

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Field Jennessa Agnew said, “Trump and his MAGA allies are doing all they can to take away voters’ right to free and fair elections while rolling back protections for our health and safety and making our lives more expensive. We’re utilizing every tool in our toolbox to mobilize voters, including those who have been historically excluded, by working alongside campaigns to reach more communities and talking about getting out the message that these candidates will fight for them, stand up to Big Polluters, and address the kitchen table issues impacting them every day.”

LCV, NRDC ACTION FUND LAUNCH AD URGING MEMBERS TO PROTECT THE CLEAN WATER ACT: LCV and NRDC Action Fund announced a six-figure ad buy to urge lawmakers to protect the Clean Water Act from further action by the Trump administration and Congress. This six-figure digital ad buy will run through October 2nd.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Trump and his allies have done everything in their power to gut critical protections for the water our communities rely on so that the fossil fuel industry, data centers, and corporate interests profit at our expense. We know the devastating costs to our health and safety when these protections fail and Big Polluters go unchecked. Families deserve clean water, no matter their income or zip code, and we’re urging members of Congress to reject polluters’ efforts to gut the Clean Water Act.”

CONGRESSIONAL DEMS INTRODUCE ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH RESTORATION ACT: Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (RI) and Jeff Merkley (OR) and Representative Sean Casten (IL-06) introduced the Environmental Health Restoration Act at a press event with Protect our Winters on Wednesday. The bill aims to restore EPA’s mission and reinstate protections for public health and the environment.

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “We appreciate Senator Whitehouse and Representative Casten for fighting to restore the EPA’s mission and safeguards to protect public health, the environment and our climate in the face of the Trump administration’s reckless and dangerous rollbacks. People want more protections for their families and our air, water, and land, not less. They want officials who will hold accountable those corrupt utilities, data center developers, and fossil fuel companies that are driving up costs and making us sicker. EPA’s leaders must fulfill the agency’s mission of protecting human health and the environment and reject President Trump’s corrupt giveaways to his tech, coal, oil, and gas cronies. LCV is proud to support the Environmental Health Restoration Act to right the ship and deliver for American families.”

SENATE AGRICULTURE COMMITTEE REPUBLICANS PASS HARMFUL FARM BILL: Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee advanced a partisan Farm Bill that would slash investments in critical programs that help farmers engage in more sustainable and regenerative farming practices while doing nothing to address the upcoming Republican-caused food security crisis.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Farmers nationwide are struggling with extreme weather and rapidly rising costs under the Trump administration. To ensure our farmers can continue putting food on tables across the country, Congress should be investing more in the programs and agencies that help farmers thrive while fighting and adapting to the climate crisis. Instead, Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee advanced a bill that slashes investments in critical, already-oversubscribed conservation programs that help farmers engage in more sustainable and regenerative farming practices and fails to address the upcoming SNAP crisis that congressional Republicans created with the Republican Tax Law. We call on the Senate to reject this harmful proposal and pass a truly bipartisan Farm Bill that supports farmers, families, and our environment.”

LCVAF ENDORSED CANDIDATES WIN DELAWARE PRIMARIES: LCV Action Fund endorsed candidates Chris Coons (Senate) and Sarah McBride (DE-AL) won their respective primary elections in Delaware. All LCV Action Fund endorsed candidates for this cycle can be found here.

LCVAF TAKE: LCV Action Fund Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Chris Coons and Sarah McBride are fighting to protect free and fair elections, the health of our communities, and a cleaner, more affordable energy future. While people are paying higher costs for gas and their energy bills due to Trump and his Republican allies’ actions, Big Polluters rake in massive profits. Voters have made it clear — they want clean air and water and affordable energy solutions. We’re all in to support candidates who will protect people and our planet.”

NEW ON THE POWER SOURCE BLOG AND SOCIALS:

ON THE BLOG: This week on the blog, we published our top five stories for fall 2026, including primary election victories, wins in the fight to rein in data centers, progress in the fight for clean energy, new laws to hold polluters accountable, and LCV Action Fund endorsements in the upcoming elections.

ON OUR SOCIALS: As energy prices soar, Secretary Wright is thankful for president Trump’s commonsense leadership. And Big Tech and Big Oil are definitely not deceiving us. Finally, it all makes sense.

COMING UP:

SEPTEMBER 21: Comment period closes on USDA’s proposal to repeal the Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

OCTOBER 5: Supreme Court oral arguments in Suncor v. Boulder.

OCTOBER 12: Indigenous People’s Day.

OCTOBER 24: National Vote Early Day.

NOVEMBER 2: Comment period closes on EPA’s proposal to not limit any climate pollution.
