text:
The U.S. Department of Energy on Sept. 3 released the 2026 U.S. Energy and Employment Report, which shows employment in corn ethanol, biomass electricity generation and “other biofuels,” which includes biodiesel and renewable diesel, expanded in 2025.

According to the report, the U.S. corn ethanol industry employed 36,100 workers last year, up 0.1% when compared to 2024. Approximately 46% of workers were employed by the agriculture and forestry industry, with 26% employed in manufacturing, 20% in wholesale trade, 7% in professional and business services and less than 1% in other services. Jobs in wholesale trade increased 6.6% between 2024 and 2025, with employment in professional and business services down 8.5%.

Overall, 56% of employers in the corn ethanol industry reported some difficulty in hiring, with 83% of those in wholesale trade reporting at least some difficulty in hiring. The occupations most difficult to hire last year included technicians or mechanical support, management, engineers/scientists.

Approximately 16% of workers in the corn ethanol industry are veterans, compared to 5% of the full U.S. workforce. Women make up 31% of the corn ethanol workforce, compared to 26% for the U.S. fuels workforce and the U.S. energy economy workforce.

The woody biomass and cellulosic biofuels industry employed 31,900 workers last year, down 5.5% when compared to 2024. Agriculture and forestry accounted for 49% of workers in the sector, followed by professional and business services at 32%, manufacturing at 15%, wholesale trade at 3% and other services at less than 1%.

Approximately 50% of employers in the woody biomass and cellulosic biofuels reported at least some difficulty in hiring last year, with 73% reporting hiring was at least somewhat difficult for professional and business services. The occupations most difficult to hire last year included engineers and scientists, management, and technicians or mechanical support.

According to the report, 15% of workers in wood biomass and cellulosic biofuels were veterans, compared to 5% of the total U.S. workforce. Women made up 32% of the workforce, compared to 26% for the U.S. fuels workforce and the U.S. energy economy.

Employment in other biofuels, defined to include renewable diesel and biodiesel, reached 42,300 last year, up 0.8% when compared to 2024. An estimated 65% of workers were employed in professional and business services, with 18% in wholesale trade, 9% in manufacturing, 7% in agriculture and forestry and less than 1% in other services.

Approximately 87% of employers in the other biofuels industry reported that hiring was at least somewhat difficult last year, particularly in professional and business services and whole sale trade, where a respective 94% and 90% of employers reported at least some difficultly in hiring. The occupations most difficult to hire last year were management, engineers and scientists, and technicians or mechanical support.

According to the DOE, 12% of workers in other biofuels were veterans, compared to 5% of the total U.S. workforce. Worman accounted for 34% of workers, compared to 26% for the U.S. fuels workforce and U.S. energy economy.

The report also highlights some data associated with bioenergy electric power generation (EGP), noting that employment expanded last year despite a decrease in generating capacity. The report said this divergence reflects new capacity expected to come online in 2026 and 2027.

title: Trump EPA to erase climate pollution limits for US coal and gas power plants
description:
The agency also asserted that pollution from U.S. power plants has "no material impact on global climate change," a position environmental and energy experts have strongly disputed.
If judges accept that argument, future administrations could face much steeper legal hurdles in trying to restore climate pollution limits, the Times reported.

text:
Federal regulators under President Donald Trump are scrapping rules that capped climate pollution from coal- and gas-burning power plants in the United States, a change with major implications for efforts to curb one of the country's biggest sources of heat-trapping gases.

Here's what to know

According to The New York Times, the Environmental Protection Agency under President Trump is withdrawing a rule from former President Joe Biden's administration that would have required many coal plants to sharply cut climate pollution by 2039 or shut down.

In announcing the rollback, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said earlier administrations had carried out a "war on coal." The agency also asserted that pollution from U.S. power plants has "no material impact on global climate change," a position environmental and energy experts have strongly disputed.

"And I still have to get an emissions test for my vehicle just to have it registered in my state and be allowed to drive it," one user commented on a Reddit post about the report.

"Full steam off the edge of the cliff, aye?" another added.

Power generation is the No. 2 source of planet-warming gases in the U.S., the Times reported. Experts also said that if the U.S. power sector were treated as its own country, it would rank as the world's fifth-biggest climate polluter.

When the Biden administration finalized its 2024 power plant rule, it estimated $120 billion in health-related benefits by 2047. For 2035 alone, the administration projected up to 1,200 fewer premature deaths, 360,000 fewer asthma attacks, and 48,000 fewer school absence days.

More background

To make the rollback stick, the EPA is pursuing two steps at once: repealing the earlier rule and arguing that the Clean Air Act does not give the agency authority to regulate pollution from power plants.

If judges accept that argument, future administrations could face much steeper legal hurdles in trying to restore climate pollution limits, the Times reported. Carrie Jenks, executive director of the Environmental & Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, said officials are "swinging for the fences" to block regulation of one of the nation's largest pollution sources.

Burning coal and gas contributes to hotter temperatures and more intense weather disasters, while power plant pollution is also linked to soot and other contaminants that can worsen breathing problems and add strain to hospitals, schools, and household budgets.

Coal had already been losing ground in the U.S. power mix, with its share of electricity generation falling from more than half in 1990 to roughly 17% in 2025. Even so, utilities are building more gas plants as electricity demand rises, including demand tied to artificial intelligence data centers.

What can be done?

The immediate fight will likely move to the courts. Several Democratic-led states and environmental groups have said they plan to challenge the EPA's move, setting up what could become another major Supreme Court fight over federal climate authority, according to the Times.

Communities and utilities still have options even without stricter federal rules. Renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, along with battery storage and energy-efficiency upgrades, can help reduce pollution while often lowering energy costs.

Reducing demand at home through weatherization, efficient appliances, and smarter cooling and heating choices can help families save money and cut the pollution tied to electricity use.

State utility decisions and public comment periods shape choices about retiring coal plants, approving new gas plants, and investing in cleaner power.

"This is another nail in the coffin for this administration's commitment to protecting people and tackling the climate crisis," said Manish Bapna, president of the Natural Resources Defense Council, per the Times.

Where can I learn more?

The rollback of climate pollution limits is part of a wider EPA effort to weaken or revisit environmental safeguards.

• Across U.S. coal country, "permits for life" on coal ash could weaken oversight.

• The EPA's air-pollution policy reversal showed how quickly protections can change across administrations.

• At the EPA, dangerous chemicals in the U.S. could stay in wider use under proposed changes.

The fight over power-plant pollution also reaches into the scientific and legal foundations of U.S. environmental policy. Federal decisions can ripple through public health, energy, and climate risks nationwide.

title: Clean tech startup Fluxnium found a way to tap 50000 years' worth of nuclear fuel
description:
Prices for yellowcake, a form of unrefined uranium, are up 75% in the last five years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
The ocean has over 4 billion metric tons of uranium in it, enough for 50,000 years or so.
“It’s like a thousand times more than all identified hard rock mines combined,” Jeff Green, founder and CEO of the clean tech Fluxnium, told TechCrunch.
Tech companies have backed several nuclear startups as they search for new sources of electricity to power their AI data centers.
The key has been to increase the surface area of the fibers, Green said.
text:
The U.S. has ambitious plans to triple the capacity of its nuclear power plants by 2050, but that goal might hit a roadblock if plant operators can’t buy fuel at reasonable prices.

Prices for yellowcake, a form of unrefined uranium, are up 75% in the last five years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Further complicating matters, the U.S. doesn’t have significant resources within its borders — unless you consider the ocean.

The ocean has over 4 billion metric tons of uranium in it, enough for 50,000 years or so. “It’s like a thousand times more than all identified hard rock mines combined,” Jeff Green, founder and CEO of the clean tech Fluxnium, told TechCrunch.

Fluxnium thinks it has solved the problem of how to extract uranium from seawater. Using technology developed at U.S. Department of Energy national labs, the company has an approach that could be competitive with existing uranium mines.

The startup has been working in stealth until now to develop the new technology. Fluxnium gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at its technology. The startup recently closed a $7 million seed round led by Congruent Ventures with participation from Active Impact Investments and Constellation Energy, which operates the largest nuclear fleet in the U.S.

Fluxnium is emerging as the nuclear industry in the U.S. undergoes a renaissance. Tech companies have backed several nuclear startups as they search for new sources of electricity to power their AI data centers.

Green’s timing is good, but perhaps not surprising. He’s a repeat founder, having helped launch Stamps.com in 1996, desalination startup NanoH2O in 2005, and carbon removal startup 1PointFive in 2020. He has a nose for where the world is going, and he thinks uranium presents a big opportunity.

While uranium isn’t rare, as elements go, uranium mines aren’t plentiful or evenly distributed. “If you’re in the West, two-thirds, three-quarters of the world’s uranium supply comes from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Russia, Namibia, Niger, China. There’s geopolitical risk.” Green said.

Those concerns have been bubbling under the surface of the nuclear industry for decades. “Now with this new nuclear renaissance?” he said. “If demand comes the way it’s being projected, we’re structurally short uranium.”

But those concerns would evaporate if someone could find a way to economically extract uranium from seawater.

Fluxnium’s technology uses specially made polymer fibers that attract the uranium that’s dissolved in seawater. The company licensed the chemistry from the Department of Energy, and it has continued to work on the production and configuration of the fibers themselves.

The key has been to increase the surface area of the fibers, Green said. When the technology was demonstrated at a national lab, it could extract uranium at more than $200 per pound, which is more than twice the price of Western suppliers today. But by increasing the surface area, Fluxnium has been able to draw more uranium out of the water, bringing costs down.

Much of the costs are wrapped up in manufacturing the fibers and deploying them in the ocean.

Here’s how it works. After the material has been made into long, braided fibers, they’re hauled out to sea and hung off buoys, similar to the way that seaweed is farmed. After 30 to 60 days at sea, they’re brought ashore, and the uranium is extracted without any toxic tailings left behind. Each line can be reused several times over.

Once the uranium is eluted from the fibers, it is purified into yellowcake. “Then we sell that just as any other mine into the supply chain,” Green said.

“None of the components of this process are anything novel. It’s all been done in different ways,” he said. “Our job is to drive cost out of the supply chain, keep working through all the stages of the process to make it as low cost as possible.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and Congressman Gary Palmer (AL-06), Chairman of the Subcommittee on the Environment, applauded the House passage of H.J. Res 210 and H.J. Res. 213 to overturn the Biden-Harris Administration’s EPA waivers that harmed the ability of ocean-going vessels and commercial harbor craft to operate in California ports.

“The Biden-Harris Administration’s EPA approved waivers allowing California to impose costly and burdensome emissions mandates—without meaningful reductions in emissions—on ocean-going tankers docked in California waters and on the ferries, tugboats, work boats, and commercial fishing boats our national economy relies on due to the importance of West Coast ports to interstate commerce. These rules are both impracticable and expensive; ultimately, they fail to achieve their emissions goals while putting new burdens on American businesses,” said Chairman Guthrie. “These waivers have a national impact, and it is important for Congress to use oversight tools like the Congressional Review Act to protect American consumers. Throughout this Congress, our Committee has continued to stand up to California’s far-left environmental overreach, and H.J. Res. 210 and H.J. Res. 213 continue that important work. Thank you to Congressman Fong and Congressman Gallagher for your leadership to overturn these unworkable California waivers.”

“California should not be allowed to dictate national environmental policy or impose its radical agenda on families and businesses across the country,” said Chairman Palmer. “As Chairman of the Environment Subcommittee, I am proud of our continued work to rein in Biden-era regulatory overreach. Passage of these resolutions will protect critical supply chains and prevent costly, impractical mandates from being passed on to American consumers.”

BACKGROUND:

Clean Air Act section 209 generally preempts states from regulating emissions from motor vehicles and other mobile sources, unless EPA grants California a waiver of preemption based on a determination that the state standards are at least as stringent as federal standards and are needed by the state “to meet compelling and extraordinary conditions.” The Clean Air Act allows other states to adopt California standards.

H.J. Res. 210:

The resolution overturns the Biden-Harris EPA’s approval of a Clean Air Act waiver allowing California to regulate emissions from ocean-going tanker ships while docked at marine terminals in California.

California regulated emissions from ocean-going container, passenger, and refrigerated cargo vessels in 2010, and the Obama EPA granted a waiver of preemption allowing those regulations to go into effect in 2011. In 2020, California amended its regulations to also cover tanker ships and roll-on/roll-off ships. EPA approved a new waiver in 2023.

These state regulations are disrupting oil imports to the state and further contributing to closures of refineries, including ones that supply critical jet fuel for military use and commercial transportation.

The technology needed to comply with state regulations does not reliably and affordably exist yet for oil tankers, making the rules impracticable and compliance virtually impossible.

H.J. Res. 213:

The resolution overturns the Biden-Harris EPA’s 2025 approval of California emissions regulations for commercial harbor craft, including ferries, tugboats, work boats, and commercial fishing boats.

The California regulations at issue require all ferries and new excursion vessels to install zero-emission and advanced technologies. For other categories of commercial harbor craft, both existing and new, the California rules would require compliance with the most stringent federal marine emission standards and use of control technologies such as diesel particulate filters that are not widely available, making compliance exceptionally difficult.

The California rules are impracticable, costly, and likely to cause unintended safety risks. Industry estimates expect the rules to impose more than $2.5 billion in costs to maritime operators and consumers without a meaningful reduction in emissions.

title: Study warns of electricity shortages unless supply keeps pace with data center growth
description:
Data center regulation and electric reliability has also become an issue in the governor’s race in November.
That’s attributable partly to increases in electric vehicle use and greater electrification in industry but mainly to data center growth.
While data centers have existed for decades, housing computers that serve e-commerce, streaming and other online services, hyperscale data centers are larger, with energy and water demands that rival those of small cities.
Under PJM’s proposal, data centers that don;t have their own power supplies would be cut off first if demand exceeds supply.
“If the grid is stressed, data centers are subject to curtailment unless you bring your own capacity,” Silverman said.
text:
Rolling blackouts would happen more than 13 days a year in a “worst case future” scenario, where data center growth is unrestrained and electricity supplies remain tight, according to a report commissioned by Pennsylvania utility regulators.

Even if new power plants are built over the next 15 years, as data center projects come online, the regional electricity grid would fall short of demands six times per decade, on average, according to the report.

“That means we’re running the grid at the red line,” Abe Silverman, a researcher at the Ralph O’Connor Sustainable Energy Institute at Johns Hopkins University, said.

The report also examines a third scenario in which no new data centers get built after 2026; it’s the only scenario in which PJM is able to achieve its reliability goal.

It delivers a blunt message, energy experts and policy makers said, that the electricity grid Pennsylvania shares with a dozen other states and Washington, D.C. needs more power quickly.

The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) released the report Monday. It examines whether sufficient electricity resources will be available to ensure the system is reliable as demand increases and older power plants retire.

“Pennsylvania is at an energy crossroads,” PUC Chairman Steve DeFrank said. “Data center development brings significant opportunities, but that growth cannot come at the expense of the families and businesses that already depend on reliable and affordable electric service.”

DeFrank added that the need to protect consumers and electric reliability is bigger than the commission.

“Pennsylvania’s energy system is changing dramatically, and our energy policies need to evolve with it,” he said, calling on policymakers, regulators, utilities, generators, consumer advocates and other stakeholders to work together toward solutions.

State lawmakers in the divided General Assembly called for swift action, but also were critical of political opponents for past decisions.

“A failure to address this growing reliability crisis will cost lives, put vulnerable Pennsylvanians at risk and cause enormous economic damage. We need to take this warning seriously and address it now,” a spokesperson for House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) said.

Spokesperson Elizabeth Rementer added the Democratic-led House passed a range of bills to speed new generation, improve efficiency and resiliency of the grid and protect consumers from additional costs.

“Unfortunately, Senate Republicans have neither considered any of these proposals nor sent meaningful legislation to the House,” she said. “We urge them to take up our legislation now to help address this impending crisis.”

Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) meanwhile placed blame for the reliability crunch on former Democratic Gov. Tom Wolf’s decision to join a regional carbon trading program, which Pittman said resulted in years of uncertainty for the power industry.

“As we look ahead, we have been clear that all sources of power should be embraced to strengthen Pennsylvania’s power grid, and I am encouraged the PUC Chairman has expressed agreement on this front and wants to ‘put as many watts on the grid as we possibly can,’” he said.

Data center regulation and electric reliability has also become an issue in the governor’s race in November. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro is seeking reelection, facing Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, who is critical of Shapiro’s early embrace of the industry.

Shapiro’s campaign, meanwhile, has hammered Garrity in TV ads over her calls for Pennsylvania to be more competitive in attracting data centers. Garrity now says she supports a pause on development and a requirement for data centers to bring their own power.

The Shapiro administration points to efforts to drive reform in PJM through public pressure, litigation, a settlement capping energy auction prices and an accord with the Trump administration on market reforms.

“Governor Shapiro is an all-of-the-above energy Governor, and he is laser focused on bringing more power to the grid while keeping costs down for the good people of Pennsylvania, who are among the 67 million consumers served by PJM,” spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky said.

Consulting firm Synapse Energy Economics found, based on grid manager PJM Interconnection’s forecast demand growth under the two scenarios, the system’s reliability would be between six and 100 times worse than PJM’s planning standard of one “loss of load” event per decade by 2030.

“PJM is lagging far behind all other U.S. grid operators in bringing on-line lower cost, quickly deployed clean energy and distributed resources that could be operational before 2030,” said Jon Gordon, senior policy director for the renewable energy industry group Advanced Energy United.

But PJM remains hamstrung by slow processes and long timelines for permitting and construction of new power plants and facilities, he said. And PJM’s “fast track” initiatives to bring new generation online quickly have focused on natural gas power plants, which face long lead times for crucial components such as turbines and transformers, he said.

“Time continues to tick away — It’s a race against the clock to try and get supply proposed, financed, permitted, and constructed, and the timelines just don’t add up right now,” Gordon said.

The report also raises the possibility that Pennsylvania could lose its status as a net exporter of electricity as more resources are retired here and new generating plants are built in other states.

Montgomery County-based PJM manages the grid spanning from New Jersey to Illinois and from the New York border to North Carolina. It is responsible for balancing supply and demand, ensuring the grid can supply the most affordable electricity available in a given location at any time. It also holds auctions for power plant owners to bid on contracts to keep power plants standing by to run when needed to meet spikes in demand.

In the last several years, it has come under criticism for allowing a backlog of electricity generation and transmission projects to pile up in its queue to connect to the grid.

At the same time, PJM forecasts its net energy load will increase 5.3% per year over the next 10 years, growing by nearly 66 gigawatts by 2036. That’s attributable partly to increases in electric vehicle use and greater electrification in industry but mainly to data center growth.

More than 80 hyperscale data centers planned to power artificial intelligence applications are planned in Pennsylvania, with about five under construction and another five with approvals. While data centers have existed for decades, housing computers that serve e-commerce, streaming and other online services, hyperscale data centers are larger, with energy and water demands that rival those of small cities.

PJM spokesman Jeff Shields told the Capital-Star the issues raised by the report have been on the organization’s radar since 2023 and that it is continuing to work with states to increase electricity supply.

Shields said PJM agrees with the PUC’s assessment that electricity demand is growing faster than the ability to build new generation and the grid’s reliability could be compromised over the next five years as electricity prices also increase. He added that the organization agrees the solution will take action at the state and federal levels and across the industry.

PJM has already embraced principles of the Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, in which it called on hyperscale data center developers to “build, bring, or buy all of the energy” they need and pay the full cost of additional infrastructure.

Pennsylvania has been an effective partner, Shields said, in efforts to streamline permitting and remove barriers for new power resources. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s administration also led litigation to establish a price cap and floor for capacity auctions; and Shapiro was among 13 state governors to join in a statement of principles in accord with PJM’s reform proposals to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).

“PJM believes these combined, focused efforts can preserve reliable electrical service in the near and long term without unfairly burdening regular ratepayers,” Shields said.

FERC is expected to rule this month on PJM’s proposal to hold a “reliability backstop auction,” in which data center operators and other large load users would be matched with investors willing to build new power plants with guaranteed buyers for their energy, Silverman said.

The commission is also expected to decide in October, Silverman added, on PJM’s proposal for a framework to connect new data centers to the grid when they have secured an energy supply in accordance with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Under PJM’s proposal, data centers that don;t have their own power supplies would be cut off first if demand exceeds supply.

“If the grid is stressed, data centers are subject to curtailment unless you bring your own capacity,” Silverman said. “We’re not going to cut off grandma if the grid gets stressed, we’re going to cut off you.”

title: When AI Hands Us Lemons, States Should Make Clean-Energy Lemonade, by Keith Raffel
description:
Even three years ago, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that generating the electricity used by U.S. data centers consumed roughly 211 billion gallons.
New York has imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers.
New data centers have also become an issue in this year's elections.
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for state and federal moratoriums on building data centers.
An AP-NORC/Energy Policy Institute poll conducted in July found 65% of Americans are in favor of requiring data centers to use clean energy.
text:
In 2026, Americans have been handed two lemons: a warming climate and an artificial intelligence data-center boom straining the nation's electricity and water systems. Maybe it's time to squeeze them together and make lemonade.

First lemon: Temperatures are rising around the world. Western Europe suffered a record heat wave this summer. Spain, for example, recorded 61 heat wave days, with Barcelona hitting 105 F, the hottest temperature since measurements began over a century ago. Researchers suspect rapid glacial melting and unusually warm conditions contributed to a catastrophic flood in Nepal.

Record heat is hitting the U.S. as well. In August, the Los Angeles suburb of Woodland Hills reached a record 111 F, while downtown LA itself tied its record of 98 F.

Scientists attribute global warming primarily to greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas. And what is the Trump administration doing about all this? Fanning the flames. It has repealed most Biden-era carbon limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants, opened 13.1 million acres of federal land to future coal mining, halted new offshore-wind leasing, and used emergency authority to keep coal-fired generating plants open.

Second lemon: The AI gold rush requires staggering amounts of electricity to operate and grow. At the end of 2025, the U.S. had 580 operational hyperscale data centers, with another 437 in the development pipeline, run by companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle. A single new gigawatt-scale AI center can consume as much electricity as a sizable city.

Unwilling to wait for more generation capacity, Elon Musk's xAI has been using 69 temporary mobile natural gas turbines at its site in Mississippi to power its data centers. The mobile turbines are relatively inefficient and can emit 40%-60% more CO2 per megawatt-hour than modern natural gas plants.

All this new demand is arriving as electricity prices are rising. Residential electricity prices nationally were 5% higher in June than they were a year earlier, with increases of more than 10% in some states, including Michigan and Pennsylvania.

On top of that, data centers can affect clean-water availability and cost, especially in arid regions and in communities where drinking water is used for cooling. Even three years ago, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that generating the electricity used by U.S. data centers consumed roughly 211 billion gallons. Although a newer national water estimate is not yet available from the lab, data-center electricity consumption has continued to climb.

New York has imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers. Legislators in 15 other states are considering similar moves. Unwilling to wait, local governments in states including Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina, Indiana, Missouri and Illinois have imposed their own stoppages.

New data centers have also become an issue in this year's elections. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for state and federal moratoriums on building data centers. Wyoming Republican U.S. House nominee Chuck Gray won his primary after campaigning to "stop data centers" and calling for a federal ban.

Lemonade: U.S. companies are racing to build these centers as they innovate and compete for leadership in AI. The projects bring investment and construction jobs, but they also impose substantial new demands on electricity and, in many cases, water.

Why then not require these hyperscale data centers to cover their added electricity demand with low- or zero-carbon generation, such as wind or solar? An AP-NORC/Energy Policy Institute poll conducted in July found 65% of Americans are in favor of requiring data centers to use clean energy.

Washington has imposed no such energy or water requirements. But states don't have to wait. They can take action now.

While the Trump administration pushes fossil fuels and curtails federal support for solar and wind power, renewable power is already competitive. With demand from leading American technology companies, accelerated investment and innovation in clean generation and storage has the potential to lower costs for all users. On top of that, state laws could help America become a leader in green energy despite the efforts of the current administration to stifle it.

States could also require data centers to reuse cooling water. For example, Microsoft and the city of Quincy, Washington, built a recycling system that treats and recirculates data-center cooling water, reducing reliance on potable groundwater by an estimated 138 million gallons a year or 97%.

It looks like it's up to the states to take action. Back in 1932, Supreme Court Justice Louis D. Brandeis wrote, "It is one of the happy incidents of the federal system that a single courageous State may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory; and try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country."

Come on, states. It's still warm out. Let's make some lemonade.

A renaissance man, Keith Raffel has served as the senior counsel to the Senate Intelligence Committee, started a successful internet software company, and had six books published including five novels and a collection of his columns. He currently spends the academic year as a resident scholar at Harvard. You can learn more about him at keithraffel.com. text:
DEARBORN, Mich. (WXYZ) — Two new playgrounds at Salina Intermediate and Elementary schools in Dearborn are now open, marking the latest additions to a $3 million green schoolyards project funded through donations and grants.

The schools, which are more than 100 years old, sit less than 800 feet from a steel factory near the Dearborn Works and the Ford Rouge Complex. School and city leaders say the natural landscaping and green infrastructure are intentional design choices meant to offset the impact of the surrounding industrial area.

WATCH VIDEO REPORT BY 7 NEWS DETROIT'S TONY GEFTOS BELOW

Dearborn schools cut ribbon on $3 million green schoolyard project

Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud said the location made the project especially meaningful.

"If you look at Salina Elementary and Intermediate School, it's less than 800 ft away from a steel factory, and so this is a prime example of how, how you want to utilize green infrastructure to help improve the air quality so our children can learn and our teachers can do what they do best," Hammoud said.

Dearborn Schools Superintendent Mike Esseily echoed that sentiment.

"Obviously the concern of the environment is global. Right here, specifically though in this part of the south end of Dearborn, it's critically important," Esseily said.

The playgrounds are also designed to serve as outdoor classrooms. Salina Elementary Principal Sue Stanley said getting students outside is a priority.

"It's really important to me to get kids outside playing and we do a lot of learning outside as well. And then the challenges of the industry next to us was also another thing," Stanley said.

Salina Intermediate School Principal Eman Ali, herself a Salina alumna, called the transformation a milestone.

"I'm -- a proud Salina alumni, proud Salina Wildcat, and seeing what has been transformed in this playscape is truly truly a dream come true," Ali said.

Students say the change is noticeable. Seventh grader Aqueel Ahmed remembered what the space looked like before.

"This was just an old basketball court with busted rims. It was nothing really over here, nothing that people used to use," Ahmed said.

Fellow seventh grader Jana Shiaab said the new equipment has already made a difference in how students spend their time.

"Because we had old equipment that was broken and not stabled, and some kids felt unsafe on them, so this new transformation helped kids go outside more and get off their electronics," Shiaab said.

Seventh grader Nawar Ali added that the environmental design has not gone unnoticed by students.

"And it's way more eco-friendly. Lots of the kids love the place," Ali said.

For fourth grader Ameer Mohamed, the answer to what he likes best was simple: the swings.

title: Rivian's ALSO e-bikes are finally hitting the road – but not for frustrated customers | Electrek
authors: Micah Toll, Fred Lambert, Peter Johnson, Jameson Dow
description:
Rivian spin-off ALSO is finally getting its futuristic TM-B electric bikes out across the United States.
Unfortunately for the customers who ordered them nearly a year ago, those bikes aren’t headed to their garages.
The company is bringing demo bikes along so prospective new customers can get an in-depth walkthrough and actually ride the TM-B before potentially placing an order.
The $4,500 Launch Edition TM-B was originally expected to begin reaching customers in spring 2026.
Hopefully, the next nationwide tour these bikes embark on will be inside delivery trucks headed to the customers who have been waiting for them.
text:
Rivian spin-off ALSO is finally getting its futuristic TM-B electric bikes out across the United States.

Unfortunately for the customers who ordered them nearly a year ago, those bikes aren’t headed to their garages. They’re headed on tour.

ALSO has kicked off its “Test Spin Fall Tour,” a traveling demo program that will bring the high-tech TM-B to cities around the country from September through November. The tour started in Portland, Oregon, and includes stops in Philadelphia, Boston, Boise, Madison, Minneapolis, Sacramento, Atlanta, Bentonville, San Antonio, Nashville, Detroit, Salt Lake City, Dallas, Tempe, and more.

The company is bringing demo bikes along so prospective new customers can get an in-depth walkthrough and actually ride the TM-B before potentially placing an order.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

While ALSO is driving TM-Bs around the country to woo new customers, many of its earliest customers are still waiting for the bikes they already paid for.

The $4,500 Launch Edition TM-B was originally expected to begin reaching customers in spring 2026. That timeline slipped into summer, then into September. Earlier this month, customers received yet another update saying Launch Edition bikes were “now shipping,” but that deliveries would occur in waves stretching all the way into early November.

As of last week, several early reservation holders on Reddit – including self-described day-one customers – were still reporting that they hadn’t received individual delivery dates.

Others have sounded the alarm about worrying signs of a stunted rollout, including multiple reports of customers visiting local bike shops listed on the ALSO site as service providers, only for the staff there to not even know they’re considered to be official ALSO service partners.

To ALSO’s credit, the company has recently made a more concerted effort to explain what has gone wrong.

Following growing criticism from customers over both the delays and a perceived lack of communication, ALSO Head of Product Saul Leiken took to Reddit with a lengthy explanation and apology.

According to Leiken, part of the problem stems from supply-chain issues affecting the raw materials used for printed circuit boards and certain integrated circuits. ALSO says demand associated with the AI boom has made some components difficult to source, in some cases forcing engineers to source and requalify alternative materials – which means more engineering and testing instead of simply swapping in another part.

There’s also the battery.

The TM-B’s removable battery is particularly unusual because it supports USB-C Power Delivery charging at up to 240W. According to ALSO’s explanation, that level of power exceeds existing regulatory guidelines for the application, requiring the company to work with standards organizations on new safety and testing protocols. The bike’s unusual DreamRide pedal-by-wire drivetrain has created another manufacturing challenge, requiring what Leiken described as high-precision production and a slower ramp to maintain quality.

Leiken acknowledged that the company should have communicated those challenges more clearly along the way.

That explanation certainly provides more context for why one of the most technologically ambitious e-bikes we’ve seen in years has proven difficult to manufacture at scale, though the company’s discussion of some of those efforts in the present tense does raise questions about the veracity of the “now shipping” claims made by ALSO earlier this month.

In all fairness, building what amounts to a software-defined light electric vehicle with a novel drivetrain and battery architecture was probably never going to be as straightforward as ordering a few hub motors and welding together some aluminum frames.

But it also creates an increasingly strange situation for ALSO’s earliest supporters.

There are apparently enough functional TM-Bs available to send fleets of them around the country so prospective buyers can take test rides. ALSO has also been operating Test Spin programs through Rivian locations, part of an effort announced earlier this year to bring demo rides to ten cities nationwide.

Meanwhile, some of the people who put down $4,500 for their e-bikes last year are still checking their inboxes for an actual delivery date.

Obviously, demo and production bikes aren’t necessarily interchangeable. Marketing fleets are allocated long in advance, and pulling a handful of demo bikes off a nationwide tour wouldn’t magically solve a production ramp involving hundreds or thousands of customer units.

But optics matter here, too.

Seeing an ALSO van roll into your city full of shiny TM-Bs has to feel a little different when you ordered yours last October and are still waiting for the email telling you when yours will arrive.

The good news is that ALSO still maintains that Launch Edition production is underway and that deliveries are coming in waves through early November.

Hopefully, the next nationwide tour these bikes embark on will be inside delivery trucks headed to the customers who have been waiting for them.

Electrek’s Take

Look, from a marketing standpoint, a tour like this makes plenty of sense. The TM-B is an impressive engineering feat, but also a pretty weird bike – in the best possible way. It probably benefits more than most from getting butts in seats. Its unconventional frame, removable top tube/seat assembly, touchscreen interface, high-powered USB-C charging, and pedal-by-wire DreamRide drivetrain make it unlike basically anything else in the e-bike industry.

These are all things you have to feel to understand. And I imagine that they feel pretty impressive, though I can’t necessarily speak from personal experience. Readers may recall that I wrote an exclusive last year ahead of ALSO’s highly anticipated and secretive launch, revealing that the company had accidentally leaked their own bike’s design from a few poorly-edited frames in a flashy teaser video. An hour later, I received an email uninviting me from the ALSO launch. So while I can appreciate the impressive engineering that went into the bike, I can’t tell you how the bike rides – at least not unless the tour stops in my city.

But from a distance, I can appreciate the dueling desires here, for a new company to get its bikes out there as broadly as possible for the public to see and ride, and to meanwhile calm frustrated customers who have no idea when they’ll get their own paid-in-full e-bikes after months of delays.

There’s no doubt that ALSO has the engineering talent to pull this off. The question is whether the other pieces of running a successful e-bike company will fall into place.

title: Most Americans Now Thinking About Electric Cars, Thanks To High Gas Prices
description:
Electric vehicles are far better than they were 5 years ago, let alone 10 or 20 or 30 years ago.
High gas prices (thanks mostly to Donald Trump’s war on Iran) have more and more Americans thinking about fuel costs, though, and thinking about switching to an electric car.
According to an annual EV Index from Here Technologies and SBD Automotive, more than 50% of surveyed drivers are now considering going electric specifically due to rising gas prices.
So, even with big consumer tax credits gone (Republicans prematurely ended the $7,500 tax credit on electric vehicles), people are thinking about going electric more and more.
For some reason, Trump has tried to claim that gas prices are up for other reasons, but the main reason for higher gas prices is — as we all know — the US war on Iran.
text:

Electric vehicles are far better than they were 5 years ago, let alone 10 or 20 or 30 years ago. They have hundreds of miles of range and are similar in cost to “comparable” gas-powered cars. In fact, if you take total cogst of ownership into account, they are often significantly cheaper. Though, most people don’t think about total cost of ownership or crunch the numbers. High gas prices (thanks mostly to Donald Trump’s war on Iran) have more and more Americans thinking about fuel costs, though, and thinking about switching to an electric car.

According to an annual EV Index from Here Technologies and SBD Automotive, more than 50% of surveyed drivers are now considering going electric specifically due to rising gas prices. So, even with big consumer tax credits gone (Republicans prematurely ended the $7,500 tax credit on electric vehicles), people are thinking about going electric more and more.

Of course, the Trump administration has also crushed federal fuel efficiency standards and CO2 emission standards, so automakers are not as motivated or required to offer electric vehicles as much as they would have been. If consumer interest in EVs grows a great deal, then, the companies that have decided to keep a focus on growing electrification should benefit and be able to scoop up a good portion of those consumers.

For some reason, Trump has tried to claim that gas prices are up for other reasons, but the main reason for higher gas prices is — as we all know — the US war on Iran. Some analyses have found that the extra cost over the life of a car could be several hundred dollars, on average.

Consumer are also now much less concerned about charging, since EV range has gone up a lot and much more charging infrastructure is in place than just a few years ago. Plus, just looking into the matter more carefully helps many people to see that it’s not a concern. About 28% of survey respondents said there were enough chargers available in 2025, whereas about 47% said so in this year’s survey. (Note that the percentage is around 85% for EV owners.)

So, overall, we should be seeing EV sales and adoption numbers going up in coming years. Though, CleanTechnica readers already expected that, right?

text:
Chinese battery manufacturing giant CATL has this week unveiled its new generation of commercial vehicle battery, the Tectrans II, which it says supports up to 1,000 kilometres of range for heavy-duty trucks as well as flexible switching between charging and battery swapping.

The new Tectrans II was unveiled at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, and comes a couple of months after local media first reported the battery’s existence.

“Commercial vehicle electrification is emerging as the third wave of the global energy transition,” said Akin Li, executive president of CATL Overseas Business.

“Across products, energy, services and ecosystem, CATL is poised to work with partners around the world to catch this third wave.”

Tectrans II has been built as a modular platform, specifically designed for diverse commercial vehicle applications and operating requirements.

In reality, this means that Tectrans II batteries can be configured in different sized battery packs, meet different energy capacity and payload requirements, is compatible with both e-axle and central-drive architectures, and supports flexible switching between charging and battery swapping.

The new Tectrans II battery supports a maximum driving range of up to 1,000 km, and can charge to 80 per cent in just 25 minutes using megawatt-level fast charging.

CATL has also standardised external dimensions, electrical interfaces, and communication protocols, allowing battery technologies and park designs to evolve as necessary. This means the batteries can work with both existing and new vehicle models without requiring major changes to the vehicle’s platform.

The modular design chosen by CATL also helps OEMs to shorten vehicle development cycles by up to half and reduce research and development costs by between 60 to 70 per cent, resulting in faster model launches and lower adaptation costs.

Increased gravimetric energy density of 170 Watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg) are around 13 per cent above the industry average, enabling vehicles to carry approximately 0.6 tonnes of additional payload at the same battery capacity.

The Tectrans II also boasts the world’s first full-tab low-impedance design, enabling 96 per cent system round-trip efficiency (RTE) and helping to reduce charging losses while delivering more usable energy for daily operations.

The battery has also been engineered for a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometre service life while maintaining 70 per cent capacity retention. Similarly, the battery also boasts robust physical protection from impacts and corrosion, a maintenance-friendly design, and three levels of system redundancy including architecture redundancy, precise fault diagnosis, and cybersecurity protection.

title: Rolls-Royce SMR Launches Supplier Programme Backed by £1.4 Billion of Contract Opportunities
description:
The launch of the Rolls-Royce SMR Supplier Programme is a major milestone in establishing a resilient, high-value UK supply chain, capable of delivering at scale and supporting our export programme.
Through strategic partnerships and greater visibility of future opportunities, the Programme will help UK suppliers engage with one of the country’s most significant clean energy projects.
Chris Cholerton, Chief Executive of Rolls-Royce SMR, said: “The scale of the opportunity available to UK suppliers from the Rolls-Royce SMR programme is very significant.
Participating suppliers will benefit from greater visibility of future supply chain requirements and access to potential opportunities across the programme.

text:
Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ) delivered the following remarks on the House Floor today in opposition to H. J. Res. 210 and H. J. Res. 213, resolutions that invoke the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to repeal two Clean Air Act waivers of federal preemption for California clean maritime standards, and block the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) from ever taking similar action in the future:

Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may consume.

I rise in strong opposition to H. J. Res. 213. Republican leadership is sending us home two weeks early for a two-month recess before the November elections, and instead of using the little time we have left to address the worsening affordability crisis that the Trump Administration is causing, we are wasting the last week of session on another round of useless Congressional Review Act resolutions.

Mr. Speaker, Trump is destroying our economy while House Republicans sit on the sidelines.

Let’s take stock of where we are, almost two years into this disastrous Administration. Sky-rocketing diesel prices above $6 a gallon – the highest price ever and getting higher every day. Trump’s reckless war of choice in Iran is costing the average household more than $3,800 from higher grocery bills and transportation costs. Gasoline prices are 35 percent higher compared to this time last year, and thanks to Trump’s disastrous tariffs, inflation has reached a three year high. With Trump’s latest trade war with Canada, costs to consumers are only going to rise further.

But rather than face any of those problems, the Republican majority is going back to the CRA well and then getting out of town.

This week’s CRAs seek to nullify common sense standards that will help save money on fuel costs and health bills. The Commercial Harbor Craft standards simply require harbor craft vessels – such as excursion vessels, tugboats, workboats, and ferries – operating within California waters, to upgrade to cleaner diesel engines or zero-emission power, depending on vessel class. And the At-Berth standards require large vessels – like container ships, tankers, cruise ships, and auto carriers – docked at California ports, to either connect to shore power or use an approved emission control strategy. Both are designed to help decrease the use of diesel fuel.

These programs have been on the books for years, driving investments in cleaner engines and technologies to upgrade port infrastructure, and saving families billions in avoided health care costs.

Repealing these programs would throw that all away so Republicans’ corporate polluter friends, like Big Oil, can take advantage of hardworking American families.

Meanwhile, these California maritime programs are making people’s lives better, and producing real benefits. The transportation sector is a major source of dangerous pollution. The Commercial Harbor Craft standards will save up to $5 billion in health care costs. And the At Berth standards are delivering more than $2 billion in public health benefits to the American people and are reducing California residents’ cancer risk by 55 percent.

If House Republicans were really concerned with costs and affordability for Americans, they would acknowledge the cost of pollution. They would recognize that to repeal these standards is to shift those costs from those responsible for generating the pollution to American workers, families, businesses, and taxpayers at a time when health care costs are also sky rocketing. The Republicans should do something about these costs, instead of doubling down on these reckless CRAs.

To top it off, once again, House Republicans are ignoring the law and abusing the CRA process to retroactively target legally authorized Clean Air Act waivers. Both the Government Accountability Office and the Senate Parliamentarian have ruled that California waivers are orders, so ineligible to be repealed with a CRA. And last week, a judge granted a preliminary injunction blocking EPA from reclassifying Clean Air Act waivers as rules and stopping the agency from sending them to Congress for nullification. But obviously the Republicans don't care, they do whatever they please just like the President, so here we are wasting floor time. I question whether these will even be sent to the Senate, to be perfectly honest.

These resolutions are a waste of our time this week and once again show that Republicans have no interest in providing much needed relief to American families.

I strongly oppose H. J. Res. 213, like I opposed H.J. Res. 210 last night and urge my colleagues to do the same. I reserve the balance of my time.

title: China E-Mobility Weekly Digest: Chinese EV Tech's New Choices and Gaps in the Global South
description:
Ethiopia offers many lessons on shifting mobility from internal combustion engines (ICE) to electric mobility, serving as a benchmark for many countries worldwide.
Chinese electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea has signed a supply agreement with electric motorcycle company Spiro for electric two-wheelers and related products.
Colombia’s TransCaribe Receives First Batch of Chinese EV Buses Chinese automakers are increasingly expanding their offerings in Latin America, with Huanghai Auto delivering the first 17 of the fifty-five new buses acquired by Cartagena’s Mayor’s Office.
The Takeaway: The shift to electric mobility in the Global South is not simply about replacing combustion engines with Chinese-made electric vehicles.
Chinese EV technology is creating opportunities for skills development and deeper localization while exposing gaps in charging, regulation, trade procedures, and accessibility.
text:
This is a free preview of the upcoming Africa EVs Weekly Digest, part of the new CGSP Intelligence service.

This week we look at Chinese electric vehicle (EV) tech through the prism of not only transitioning mobility but also accessibility, usability, and inclusivity for people living with disabilities.

Ethiopia offers many lessons on shifting mobility from internal combustion engines (ICE) to electric mobility, serving as a benchmark for many countries worldwide.

For this reason, the country is hosting the annual Nordic-Africa EV Summit, a twin-city event series held between Addis Ababa and Oslo, two of the world’s most electrically mobile cities outside China. Addis, an African city, stands out because its electrification rates surpass those of many Western cities.

The Summit, currently underway in Addis, is a matchmaking event for mobility transition stakeholders in transport, energy systems, and battery energy storage. This differs from many Chinese events, which focus mostly on sales rather than the entire EV ecosystem.

As a lead-up to this event, I joined a team of Kenyan electric mobility enthusiasts in an EV experiment to drive ~1,600 kilometers from Nairobi to Addis using electric buses. Although I only reached the border town of Moyale, 780 kilometers north of Nairobi, the drive was instructive. I realized that one key factor that has not quite hit home in the e-mobility shift is the need to incorporate the needs of people living with disabilities who need assistive technology to help them move, increasing their independence and contribution to society.

For public transport access, think of well-maintained tactile paving, the textured paths that blind and visually impaired people use, while also integrating audio signage to help them navigate cities unaided. For wheelchair users, buses with platforms that can be raised or lowered could help them board without leaving their wheelchairs. So far, little has happened in this area, even with electric buses.

This need came out during the trip when I spoke with Bernard Chiira, co-founder and director of Innovate Now, Africa’s premier assistive technology accelerator. As a person living with disability, he noted that the electric mobility shift needs to address limited mobility needs, along with its focus on charging networks and other infrastructure.

To get to Moyale, we used fully electric, Chinese-made Kinglong buses, locally assembled in Kenya by BasiGo. Along the way, we swapped buses and drivers thrice because the battery range was limited to 300 kilometers. The drivers, all trained afresh to handle the electric buses, were keen not to drain the batteries, which could have meant being stuck on the road until rescued.

Driving through Kenya’s highlands, savannah, and the Chalbi Desert as part of the Kenyan team opened my eyes to what real e-mobility awareness and inclusivity are all about. And, in my opinion, I don’t think many buyers really understand what it requires to own an EV, particularly when it comes to long distances. I will share more details in an upcoming piece that breaks down the challenges and opportunities in the broader e-mobility shift.

For now, here are the latest updates in the EV sector across some of the countries in the Global South.

This week in the Chinese EV scene:

Ghana Eyes EV Skills Center as China’s Electric Truck Numbers Grow

As Chinese electric trucks gain traction in Africa, Ghana is seeking to establish an EV skills center as heavy-truck numbers continue to grow. Ghana’s Lands and Natural Resources Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah says Ghanaian mechanics need effective training to service EVs.

Why This Matters: As one of the earliest adopters of electric vehicles, this proposal could point to the country’s approach to addressing gaps in the sector as well as creating job opportunities in a sector that is increasingly mainstream.

Cape Town’s Clicks Group Launches 30 Electric SANY Trucks

South Africa’s logistics company, Clicks, has introduced 30 SANY heavy-duty electric trucks to serve its key national distribution nodes. The launch includes fast-charging capabilities through a power infrastructure directly integrated with site solar microgrids for seamless, zero-downtime charging during cargo offloading.

Why This Matters: Logistics remains one of the most challenging sectors to electrify. Growing awareness and expanding charging networks could make South Africa a reference point for other players looking to green the most polluting transport sector.

Chinese Subsidiary, GZ-AUTO, Launches Dealership in Abidjan

GZ-AUTO, a subsidiary of the Guangzheng Industrial Investment Group, has inaugurated its flagship and regional headquarters for West Africa in Treichville, Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The company will deal with various Chinese auto brands, including BYD, Changan, Jetour, Great Wall, and Equation Leopard, among others.

Why This Matters: As competition heats up at home, Chinese automakers are finding alternative markets through partnerships with players across the Global South. This will not only open these markets by building brand awareness but also increase competition, which should translate into better-quality vehicles at affordable prices in price-sensitive markets.

Chinese electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea has signed a supply agreement with electric motorcycle company Spiro for electric two-wheelers and related products. Spiro will integrate the vehicles into its proprietary battery-swapping and energy infrastructure.

Why This Matters: Beyond mere supply, Yadea and Spiro will also co-develop customized two-wheeler platforms suited to local conditions. The partnership follows a broader trend: localization partnerships are increasingly important, rather than importing fully built units.

Egypt, China’s CATL to Build 5 GWh Battery Plant

Egypt’s BME Battery Manufacturing Company has signed an agreement with China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) to build a battery manufacturing facility in the country.

The project will begin with an initial production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) annually, with the first phase focusing on battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles before increasing capacity to 5 GWh to include production of passenger vehicle batteries and energy storage systems for solar and wind power projects.

Why This Matters: Beyond local manufacturing, such partnerships also lay the groundwork for deeper localization through skills transfer. While technology transfer may take time to formalize, the skills learned in such establishments will equip locals for local ventures in similar fields.

XPeng to Officially Launch Two Models in the Philippines

Following its earlier announcement of a third-quarter entry into the local market, XPeng Philippines will finally launch the XPeng X9 and XPeng L03 on September 25, 2026. The vehicles are priced at PHP 4.058 million and PH 2.058 million, respectively.

Why This Matters: After delivering 62,682 vehicles in the first quarter of 2026 alone, XPeng’s expansion into the Philippines shows that Chinese automakers are increasingly targeting markets outside China, raising the possibility of cutthroat competition spilling into these new markets. This could mean more options for buyers in the Global South and signal to financiers to expand financing options.

Shacman Introduces Hybrid and EV Trucks in Indonesia

Indonesia’s MC Group has introduced SHACMAN hybrid and EV trucks, including the SHACMAN X5000 EV Dump Truck 8×4 580 HP at the Mining Indonesia 2026 expo. The companies also signed three cooperation agreements, with a planned procurement of 400 SHACMAN vehicles.

Why This Matters: Indonesia supplies more than half of the world’s mined nickel and serves as the primary foundation for China’s stainless steel and electric-vehicle battery supply chains. The introduction of these EV trucks could make nickel mining more energy- and cost-effective, potentially moderating the carbon footprint of an infamously polluting industry.

DP World’s Record BYD EV Shipment to Chile

1,918 fully electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles arrived in San Antonio, Chile, marking the first call by a BYD car carrier at a Chilean port. The vehicles will be distributed across Chile.

Why This Matters: As international EV demand rises, so do shipping needs. This creates an opportunity for logistics companies to evolve and innovate, including in EV shipping capacity and delivery times.

Colombia’s TransCaribe Receives First Batch of Chinese EV Buses

Chinese automakers are increasingly expanding their offerings in Latin America, with Huanghai Auto delivering the first 17 of the fifty-five new buses acquired by Cartagena’s Mayor’s Office.

Why This Matters: As a crude oil exporter, Colombia’s shift to e-mobility is interesting because it imports refined petroleum products. Shifting public transport to electric could help the country build a dual system of electric and hydrocarbon transportation, which could accelerate weaning itself off imported fuel.

In Context:

Chinese electric-vehicle technology is increasingly becoming common across customized platforms, supported by manufacturing partnerships that make it more useful in local conditions. As e-mobility companies customize their offerings, accessibility is another key area that needs attention.

The Takeaway:

The shift to electric mobility in the Global South is not simply about replacing combustion engines with Chinese-made electric vehicles. It is about building systems that work across borders, transport modes, and the needs of different users. Chinese EV technology is creating opportunities for skills development and deeper localization while exposing gaps in charging, regulation, trade procedures, and accessibility.

text:
The Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources heard testimony Wednesday on the Energy Efficiency Reform Act. The new bill would make it much more difficult for the Department of Energy to update energy efficiency standards for home appliances like dishwashers, washing machines and boilers. It would also set a path for the department to backslide on existing energy efficiency mandates.

Through the federal Appliance and Equipment Standards Program, which was authorized under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, the Department of Energy sets binding minimum efficiency standards for electricity and water consumption for a variety of home and industrial products. The department reviews an appliance’s standards every six years at a minimum. The standards are intended to provide uniform requirements across the country and “to promote grid resiliency and reliability by reducing peak demand,” according to a factsheet the Department of Energy released last year.

Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), with the backing of the Department of Energy, wants to make sweeping changes to this program, establishing significant hurdles to setting new efficiency standards.

“At the end of the day, it’s about giving Americans the choice—the freedom to choose what works best for them and their family,” said Lee, the bill’s sponsor, during the hearing.

Despite acknowledging the cost savings of past efficiency standards, Lee said the new law would provide consumers with more flexibility and freedom of choice when it comes to prices—points which were echoed by Associate Deputy Secretary of Energy Alex Fitzsimmons. He also said current policies force standards reviews “even when there may be few efficiency gains left to squeeze out of the product after it’s already been improved.”

Congressional Democrats argued, in an August letter to Secretary of Energy Chris Wright concerning other rollbacks to efficiency standards policies, that the law, as written, “already requires proving that new product standards yield significant energy- and cost-savings without imposing strict consumer choice limitations.”

The Appliance Standards Awareness Project, a nonprofit that works to advance new appliance standards, estimates American households have saved an average of $6,000 on their utility bills over the past decade because of these standards. According to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, these standards are estimated to have saved what amounts to 6.5 percent of total U.S. energy consumption in 2024 alone.

“Our view is that technology keeps improving, and the job of the efficiency standards program is to ensure that technologies that can reduce costs for consumers show up in the full range of products in the marketplace,” said Andrew deLaski, the executive director of the Appliance Standards Awareness Project.

Lee’s bill would create more obstacles to setting a new efficiency standard, like adding more steps to the process of approving a new standard, and making the energy department’s periodic review of a product’s standards voluntary.

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), who caucuses with Democrats, said changes to the existing law could end up costing Americans by making them miss out on savings at a time when energy bills are stubbornly high.

The new bill doesn’t just make it harder to establish new standards, it also makes it easier to cancel old ones—a big concern for manufacturers’ associations.

In a statement, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association said the current rules that prevent backsliding on efficiency standards means manufacturers make long-term investments to meet them. If these standards can be more easily repealed, the statement said, that could limit consumer utility bill savings and strand manufacturer investments.

The ranking member of the Senate committee, Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), said the repeal of efficiency standards could undermine domestic manufacturing, allowing Chinese manufacturers to sell less efficient, cheaply made products in the American market.

The Appliance and Equipment Standards Program has had mostly bipartisan support since 1975. But during his first term, President Donald Trump changed the process through which the Department of Energy establishes new efficiency standards. President Joe Biden reversed most of the new policies—and now the Department of Energy is trying to reinstate them, and adding even more changes to “permanently end home green new scam appliance mandates.”

The bill now before the Senate committee would codify the changes to the process, making it more difficult for a future administration to reverse them.

“They’re putting up so many hurdles and barriers to new standards that they’re making them all but impossible,” said deLaski. “I would argue they’re essentially impossible.”

When will we see new GM hybrids with more than two seats in North America?
text:
If you follow the stock market at all, you’re probably still kicking yourself for not dropping $10k into Sandisk last year. If you’d done that in April 2025 and cashed out 14 months later you’d have made almost $800k. It could be worse though: You could be GM and have invested billions in EVs only to discover everyone wants hybrids.

Rewind to the late 2010s and the whole car industry was going gaga for EVs, with multiple brands pledging to go electric-only by 2030 and most putting huge resources into battery-powered cars. Growing EV sales figures and tightening regulations really did make electric vehicles look like they would take over the world.

Related: Kia Sets All-Time August Sales Record As Hybrids Soar

Hybrids, meanwhile, which had kick-started the modern electric revolution in the late 1990s, were dismissed as an “interim solution” by GM boss Mary Barra in 2019, Reuters reminds us. But seven years later, American car sales say hybrids are the complete solution, not an interim one. And automakers who bet on gasoline-electric rather than electric power alone are winning big.

The biggest winner is Toyota. It’s crushing the competition, securing a 49.2 percent share in Q1 of the hybrid market, Cox Automotive says, per Reuters. That market has grown, too. Hybrids’ share of the total car market swelled from 16 percent in February to 19 percent in August on account of gas prices exploding following the start of war in Iran. And one analyst told Reuters he expects hybrids to hit a 34 percent share by 2031.

Stuck To Its Hybrid Guns

Toyota, you’ll remember, popularized the hybrid with the original Prius, and endured years of criticism for being slow to launch EVs. But it never wavered from its commitment to hybrids, and that determination is paying off in the US in 2026. While GM’s share of the US car market fell from 17.6 percent in the first half of 2025 to 16.8 percent in the same period this year, Toyota’s grew from 15.5 to 15.8 percent, according to Cox Automotive.

EVs also cut fuel costs, of course. And in Europe, which is suffering the same kind of gas pain American drivers are battling, EV sales are on fire. One in every four new cars sold there is an EV. But in the US, sales are heading in the opposite direction, partly as a result of the Trump administration killing federal EV tax credits. Their share of the US market fell from 14.4 percent in September 2025 to 7.1 percent this May.

The 19 MPG Hybrid

So if GM wants to get back in the game, it’s got no option but to deliver multiple new hybrid choices to support the straight gas vehicles it fortunately kept building. Incredibly, the General’s sole hybrids in the US today are two Corvettes, the $111k E-Ray and $227k ZR1X, though in previous years it also sold hybrid sedans and SUVs. It also sells hybrids in China.

When will we see new GM hybrids with more than two seats in North America? Dealers won’t like the answer, because while the automaker won’t confirm dates or comment on speculation, Reuters industry sources say American showrooms could be hybrid-free zones until near the end of the decade.

text:
By Martin McConnell

The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) has absorbed the Coalition for Community Solar Access (CCSA) in a move the associations say will expand their combined network and enhance their total capabilities.

The move comes following approval from the Boards of Directors from both organizations, representatives say. The official move will allow the organizations to coalesce into one, forming the only American trade association representing every segment of the solar and energy storage industry.

“By bringing CCSA into SEIA, we’re creating a stronger, more unified voice for the solar and storage industry,” says Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA. “Together, we’ll build on CCSA’s success and become a more powerful advocate for every segment of the industry.”

The combined organization will represent companies across the residential, commercial, utility-scale, and community sectors of the solar industry. The two associations aim to form “a single, powerful voice for solar and storage,” driving continued growth and expansion of resources across the U.S.

A crucial political moment

Solar and storage are continuing to expand their respective roles in the American energy ecosystem, SEIA officials say. Storage especially has become a necessity for many solar projects in the U.S., as grid reliability and distributed energy resources become high priorities throughout the industry.

Additionally, the solar landscape is constantly on high alert for change under the second Trump administration.

The “solar coaster” has perhaps never been bumpier in the modern era, and SEIA says this critical moment is perfect for its integration with CCSA. The associations aim to create a network that can “shape market and policy priorities at both the state and federal levels,” officials say.

“A little more than a decade ago, CCSA was formed to create greater access to solar for all Americans. Today, as distributed community power has become one of the most credible solutions to affordability and grid reliability, so has the need for greater scale, resources, and expertise to meet the moment,” says Jeff Cramer, the departing CEO of CCSA. “I am deeply proud of the work we have done, the team we built, and the industry we helped shape, and equally excited to see it evolve inside SEIA.”

SEIA says the integration of CCSA’s team, resources, and political body of work will take place by early October.

text:
Fast-charging G CELLS from Graphene Manufacturing Group (GMG) have run 489 charge and discharge cycles without measurable capacity loss, according to test data collected by the Battery Innovation Center of Indiana (BIC) and current as of September 4, 2026. The 1 Ah pouch cells were charged and discharged within six minutes for each cycle, at a 10 C rate in both directions.

BIC built the test cells itself, using graphene materials that GMG developed, manufactured and supplied from its Brisbane Battery Development Centre. The work falls under a joint development agreement between GMG and Rio Tinto.

GMG’s product page describes G CELLS as graphene aluminum-ion cells that use no lithium or rare earth materials, and says they are designed to be interchangeable with lithium-ion battery applications.

A lithium titanate oxide (LTO) cell put through the same profile fell to 86% of its original capacity within 64 cycles. GMG puts the difference at more than seven times the cycle life under identical testing.

Internal resistance of the G CELLS measured around 5 mΩ, against up to 30 mΩ for the LTO cell. Lower resistance means less resistive heating at a given current. The G CELLS ran 4° C above ambient during testing, and the LTO cells ran 19° C above it.

GMG reports specific energy lower than it has previously reported. The company describes the cells as unoptimized and expects to bring the figure back to around 50 Wh/kg at the same charge rate after further optimization.

Voltage stayed close to flat across roughly 80% of the discharge, which GMG says makes constant-power discharge easier to control.

“Having built and scaled battery manufacturing for the world’s largest lithium-ion producer, I know how rare it is to see this combination of fast-charge durability and thermal control this early in a cell’s development,” said Bob Galyen, GMG Director and former Chief Technology Officer of CATL. “There is clear further work ahead on some of the energy density optimisation and further scaling of the cell size, but the fundamentals being demonstrated here are the right ones to be solving first.”
